items.abstract: Aim To analyze research landscapes, hotspots, and trends in artificial intelligence (AI) applied to ophthalmic optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) from 2015 to 2024, aiming to reveal global collaborations and guide future research. Methods We retrieved publications from Web of Science Core Collection using AI and OCTA-related search terms. After screening, 237 articles were analyzed with CiteSpace (version 6.3.R1) for co-citation, collaboration, and keyword burst analysis. Results Annual publications grew rapidly since 2017. China (94 publications) and the US (86 publications) were the most productive and influential countries. Research focused on: deep learning algorithms and vessel segmentation, ocular disease diagnosis including diabetic retinopathy and glaucoma, and automated vascular quantification and multimodal imaging. Key limitations included small sample sizes and limited algorithm generalizability. Conclusion The integration of AI with OCTA has significantly advanced the automation and precise quantitative analysis of ophthalmic vascular imaging, demonstrating substantial potential for diagnosing various retinal and choroidal diseases. Future efforts should focus on developing more robust and interpretable AI models, conducting large-scale, multi-center clinical validation, and establishing standardized imaging and analysis protocols to ultimately realize the widespread adoption of AI-OCTA technology in routine clinical practice.

items.abstract: Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) exhibits extensive genetic diversity, posing a major challenge to AIDS vaccine development. Broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs) isolated from HIV-1-infected individuals offer valuable templates for designing broadly protective immunogens. Here, structural and energetic descriptors extracted from experimentally resolved bNAb/HIV-1 Envelope (Env) protein-protein complexes were used to develop machine-learning (ML) models predicting binding free energies (∆G) and dissociation constants (KD) across multiple HIV-1 clades. Among the algorithms evaluated, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) achieved the best predictive performance, with training and test R2 values of 0.92 and 0.658, respectively. Applying the optimized model to HIV-1 datasets revealed clade-dependent binding patterns, with clade B showing the greatest variability and clade G exhibiting signatures associated with reduced neutralization potency. Predicted ∆G of different bNAb classes followed the trend gp120-gp41 interface ≈ fusion domain > CD4 binding site (CD4bs) > V1V2 loop ≈ V3-glycan, consistent with experimentally reported affinity profiles of benchmark bNAbs. Clade C exhibited intermediate ∆G with PGT121, VRC01, and 10-1074 maintaining high-affinity interactions, whereas PG9 and 2G12 show reduced binding affinity. These findings offer quantitative insight into clade-specific bNAb binding energetics and demonstrate the potential of machine-learning approaches to guide HIV-1 immunogen design and vaccine development.

items.abstract: Summary: Thus far, evidence for drug repurposing is contained in target-, drug-, trial-, and literature-based data sources that are challenging to synthesize for non-specialists. Here, we introduce RePurpose, a web-based tool that takes as input a topic written in plain language and returns candidate drugs built from data in Open Targets, ClinicalTrials.gov, UniProt, and PubMed. For queries in the form of a goal, RePurpose filters candidate drugs by whether they modulate all targets implicated in the goal in the corresponding direction. Every candidate has a source that contributes evidence: a structured database, a clinical trial, or a proposal from a large language model. An adjustable ranking adjusts the order of candidates from well-studied to less well-known candidate drugs. We retrospectively tested RePurpose with the trial drug clemastine, which was being considered as a remyelinating agent in multiple sclerosis (MS). RePurpose retrieved clemastine in each replicate of the mechanism-worded queries, but in no replicates of the disease-worded queries, and no structured query retrieved it without the language model enabled. Its ranked outputs reflected the evidence supporting clemastine but not later evidence of harm in progressive MS, which was reachable only through an on-demand literature search. Our results imply that RePurpose may be better at tracing evidence around a hypothesis than generating new hypotheses. Availability and Implementation RePurpose Pharma is freely accessible at https://www.repurposepharma.com/. For code and more information on the application, see: https://github.com/nayagamnitin-hub/RePurpose-Pharma.

items.abstract: Abstract This systematic review made a bold attempt to examine artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) applications in drug discovery, addressing a fragmented literature characterized by inconsistent terminology and limited benchmarking. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, Scopus, PubMed, and Web of Science were queried (January 2019-August 2026). The three databases returned 23,404 records; after removing 4,491 duplicates and multi-stage screening, 618 peer-reviewed studies were included. Quality was assessed using a ROBINS-I-inspired framework across four dimensions (methodological rigor, dataset transparency, reproducibility, evaluation validity); 38 studies (6.1%) were double-coded (\((\kappa = 0.74)\)). Machine learning and deep learning dominated (99.8% and 78.0%, respectively). QSAR/CADD appeared in 58.9%, GNN/GCN in 45.1%, and Transformer/LLM architectures in 45.5%, with 99.8% of transformer papers published in 2024–2026. Virtual screening was most common (57.1%), followed by de novo design (30.6%) and drug-target interaction prediction (13.8%). The most prominent challenges were integration and clinical translation (15.2%), interpretability (11.3%), and benchmark/validation (9.2%). AUC-ROC dominated reporting (12.9%), while F1 (0.8%) and recall (0.5%) were severely under-reported-problematic for heavily imbalanced bioactivity datasets. Methodological rigor was generally high (68%), but dataset transparency (45%) and reproducibility (38%) were weaker; external validation was rare (<25%), and moderate-to-high selection bias was identified in 42% of studies. The review produced a two-axis taxonomy, a five-phase temporal framework, and a benchmarking synthesis. Priority directions include molecular foundation models, multimodal integration, autonomous AI-robotics laboratories, and federated learning. No funding was received, and the review was not prospectively registered.

items.title: Integrated In Silico, Population-Genomic and In Vitro Characterization of Three Rare CYP21A2 Missense Variants (p.A90V, p.L108Q and p.L318M) Resolves Their Role in Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia by 21-Hydroxylase Deﬁciency
items.summary: Background: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in CYP21A2. items.abstract: Background: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in CYP21A2. Although well-established genotype-phenotype correlations exist for the common pseudogene-derived alleles, next-generation sequencing increasingly identifies rare missense variants whose clinical significance is unknown, which hampers classification, counselling and the selection of patients for new targeted therapies. Methods: We characterized three CYP21A2 missense variants reported in patients with non-classic (NC) or simple-virilizing (SV) CAH, p.A90V (c.269C>T), p.L108Q (c.323T>A) and p.L318M (c.952C>A), together with the intron 2 splice variant c.293-13C>G (I2G) found in trans in two of the patients. Variants were annotated at the gene level with NCBI E-utilities (ClinVar, dbSNP), Ensembl VEP, SpliceAI and AlphaGenome, at the population level with gnomAD v4.1 and the 1000 Genomes Project, and at the protein level with AlphaMissense, REVEL, CADD, MetaRNN, PrimateAI, evolutionary conservation, AlphaFold and FoldX stability calculations mapped on the CYP21A2 crystal structure. Wild-type and variant enzymes were expressed in HEK293T cells, protein levels were quantified by Western blot, and 21-hydroxylase activity was measured with radiolabelled progesterone and 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP) followed by thin-layer chromatography. Results: All three missense variants are absent from or singletons in 1.6 million gnomAD alleles, absent from the 1000 Genomes Project and absent from ClinVar, affect residues that are conserved in mammalian orthologues and lie in high-confidence regions of the AlphaFold model (pLDDT 97-99). AlphaMissense classified p.A90V and p.L108Q as likely pathogenic (0.76 and 0.85) but p.L318M as likely benign (0.31), whereas CADD, MetaRNN and REVEL supported deleteriousness for all three; SpliceAI and AlphaGenome excluded a splicing effect of the missense changes but reproduced the acceptor-site loss and cryptic-acceptor activation caused by I2G. In vitro, protein expression was reduced to 52%, 65% and 59% of wild type for p.A90V, p.L108Q and p.L318M. Total 17-OHP 21-hydroxylation was 36.7%, 1.4% and 38.5% of wild type, and total progesterone conversion 24.9%, 9.2% and 17.5%, revealing a substrate-dependent, almost complete loss of function for p.L108Q. FoldX predicted destabilization for p.A90V (ΔΔG 3.2 kcal/mol) and p.L108Q (2.5 kcal/mol) but not for p.L318M (0.1 kcal/mol); structural analysis attributes the severe p.L108Q defect to disruption of the hydrogen-bond network (L108-G111-R427) that anchors the heme propionates. Conclusions: Combining functional assays with gene- and protein-level computational analysis classifies all three variants as pathogenic. p.L108Q is a severe allele consistent with classic SV CAH, which resolves the ambiguous SV/NC classification of the male index patient, whereas p.A90V (homozygous) and p.L318M (in trans with I2G) are mild alleles that explain the NC phenotypes. The data illustrate that AlphaMissense alone would have misclassified p.L318M and that residual activity, not in silico scores, should guide counselling and the selection of patients for CRF1-receptor-antagonist therapy.

items.abstract: In medical imaging AI, we commonly assume that diagnostic classifiers will increase in accuracy if they are trained on more data, but in reality, their performance often plateaus. To understand this behavior, we ran a spectral analysis of 3D vision transformers, a common supervised deep learning model that can be trained to classify disease based on 3D brain MRI. For simpler classification methods such as linear discriminant analysis, the classifier performance AUC(N), when trained on a sample of size N, is known to depend on the encoder′s eigenspectrum. Each class-discriminative direction in the latent space contributes only after the sample size N reaches a threshold, so the spectrum influences how performance scales with training data. Building on this theory, we show that supervised transformers compress almost all of their discriminative signal into one principal component (EVR@1 = 0.90—0.96): after this representation collapse happens, no further directions cross the threshold as training data increases, and accuracy plateaus. In principle, this plateau in performance could be due to either the encoder′s learned feature space or the difficulty of the task. To distinguish these cases, we trained three types of supervised 3D transformers (ViT3D, MINiT, NIT) and, as a non-collapsing alternative, a frozen self-supervised encoder (DINO), to classify people with dementia or mild cognitive impairment (MCI) versus cognitively normal (CN) individuals from 3D brain MRI, using data from the Alzheimer′s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). We froze each encoder and applied it to a new task, so that only the task difficulty varied. An easy task encoder (Dementia vs CN), transferred to the harder task (MCI vs CN), did not reproduce the plateau (MINiT threshold 9.2), but full retraining did (2758.5). The plateau is therefore due to the learned encoder, rather than task difficulty. Ranking the feature directions by the proportion of the disease signal they contain, we were able to identify a sign of representation collapse, i.e., a single dominant spike in the latent feature eigenspectrum. This spike was 11—26 times larger than predicted from the rest of the spectrum for the disease-trained (supervised) encoders, but was absent for DINO (0.66). To predict how transformer accuracy scales with the number of training scans, a large spike in the encoder spectrum suggests that the representation has collapsed and additional scans will not help; a small spike means that the signal is spread across many encoder latent space directions, and more training data should boost the classifier performance.

items.abstract: Protein immunogenicity is a major cause of biologic drug failure, leading to the production of anti-drug antibodies (ADA) that accelerate drug clearance, rejection of repeated doses, abolished efficacy, and sometimes life threatening anaphylaxis in patients. These responses constrain the clinical use of synthetic protein therapeutics from non-human origin. To efficiently deimmunize protein therapeutics, we developed a generative discrete diffusion model (MESSI), which takes protein structures as input and outputs sequences that preserve structure without containing peptides predicted to bind major histocompatibility complex class II molecules. MESSI designs sequences with high structural recovery and down to 0 predicted epitopes for specified MHC molecules at higher efficiency than post-hoc filtering approaches. Experimentally, we first applied MESSI to deimmunize a luciferase and a de novo designed mini-binder against PD-1, resulting in variants with no predicted epitopes and higher activity than their parents. Lastly, we coupled MESSI with evolution guidance to deimmunize uricase, a clinically approved enzyme with severe immunogenicity, and found deimmunized variants with higher catalytic activity than their natural orthologs. MESSI enables generative design of functional proteins with minimized immunogenicity, potentially making protein therapeutics safer and more effective.

items.abstract: Rare diseases can remain undiagnosed for years because individual disorders are uncom-mon and clinically heterogeneous, while relevant clues are distributed across structuredphenotypes, facial appearance, prior cases and disease knowledge. Computational toolscan use Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO)-encoded findings, genomic data and increas-ingly diverse medical images, but these modalities are processed by models with differentoutputs and score scales. ZebraSeek converts clinical and facial inputs into ranked diseasecandidates with specialist tools, then uses a large language model (LLM) to integrateand externally check those candidates while retaining their sources. Facial-image analysisprovides a complementary machine-readable phenotype that can capture patterns notfully represented by manually encoded HPO terms. In 74 literature-derived cases spanning19 diseases, ZebraSeek placed the recorded diagnosis first in 50 (67.6%) and within fivein 59 (79.7%); it recovered 11 diagnoses outside PubCaseFinder’s top five, while fivediagnoses present in PubCaseFinder’s top five were absent from ZebraSeek’s final top five.During DBCLS BioHackathon 2026, we expanded analysis to 368 patients, 462 imagesand 54 disorders to examine how candidate depth affects coverage and downstreamcandidate count, and to assess the feasibility of case-specific candidate selection.

items.abstract: Abstract The growing volume and complexity of heterogeneous medical data create challenges in extracting diagnostic knowledge while preserving privacy because centralized models face high computation costs and security risks. To overcome this limitation, the novel Asynchronous Federated Multi-Convolution Spatial and Efficient Squeeze-Excitation Network (AFL-MCSESEN) with Bulyan-Based Adaptive Differential Privacy (BADP) was proposed for Privacy-Preserving Multi-Modal Data Fusion in Sustainable AI-Driven Healthcare Systems (HS) (AFL-MCSESEN-BADP-HS). Initially, Multi-modal data such as structured, semi-structured, and unstructured Knee Osteoarthritis data are collected and stored in Apache Spark managed by data lake. These heterogeneous sources are integrated using the Unified Element Tree Fusion method. Then, these fused data are processed through Z-score normalization and feature vector encoding. Simultaneously, the knee joint images are standardized for attaining consistent visual representation of pathological changes. Then, these pre-processed inputs are processed for Local Feature Extraction and Refinement using a Multi-Convolution Spatial and Efficient Squeeze-Excitation Network. Here, ResNet-34 backbone integrated with a Condensed Depthwise Squeeze-Excitation (CDSE) module and Multi-Convolution Spatial Attention (MCSA) was utilized to isolate subtle clinical indicators. To maintain institutional privacy, these features are trained within an privacy-preserving asynchronous federated learning framework, where ten institutional clients compute local gradients on vertically partitioned data using secure inner-product evaluations. Finally, a Bulyan-Based Adaptive Differential Privacy mechanism is utilized for further enhancing robustness and privacy. By this, the proposed AFL-MCSESEN-BADP-HS system provide sustainable, high-accuracy diagnostic tool for classifying Kellgren-Lawrence (KL) Grades of Knee Osteoarthritis such as Grade 0 (Healthy), Grade 1 (Doubtful), Grade 2 (Mild), Grade 3 (Moderate) and Grade 4 (Severe). Here, the proposed AFL-MCSESEN-BADP-HS system attains an Accuracy of 99.64%, an Area Under curve value as 0.998, Communication Overhead as 285MB, Data Integration Latency as 703.33ms, Spark Query Throughput as 516.67QPS, Attack Success Rate as 1.8 and Privacy-Utility Index (PUTI) as 0.96. By this results, the proposed AFL-MCSESEN-BADP-HS system provides the promising solution for Privacy-Preserving Healthcare Systems.

items.abstract: Abstract Background Dental calculus is a primary etiological factor in periodontal disease, disproportionately affecting underserved populations with limited access to professional dental care. Automated photographic oral disease screening tools may help bridge this access gap by enabling early identification of calculus burden in community, school-based, and remote settings. Methods A ResNet-50 encoder integrated within a U-Net segmentation architecture was trained on intraoral photographic images sourced from a public dataset. The dataset was partitioned into training (1,361 images; 66.5%), validation (584 images; 28.5%), and an independent held-out test set (103 images; 5.0%), with the test set withheld from all model development decisions. Manual polygon segmentation masks were created using CVAT. A pixel-area calculation technique was developed to estimate the percentage of tooth surface covered by calculus. Architecture comparisons were conducted against a standard U-Net (no pretraining), VGG16/U-Net, and EfficientNet-B4/U-Net under identical training conditions. Results On the held-out test set, the model achieved a Dice coefficient of 0.731 (95% CI: 0.706–0.756), IoU of 0.698 (95% CI: 0.671–0.724), recall of 0.714, and specificity of 0.971. The pixel-level ROC-AUC was 0.931 (95% CI: 0.918–0.944) however, this value is inflated by background pixel dominance and should be interpreted alongside Dice and IoU as primary segmentation metrics. The proposed architecture outperformed all three comparators. Validation-set metrics (Dice 0.743, IoU 0.712) were modestly higher than test-set values, as expected given reduced optimization bias on unseen data. Conclusions This proof-of-concept study demonstrates that deep learning can support automated dental calculus screening from photographic images. Findings are preliminary and subject to important limitations including non-clinician annotation and a single public dataset source. With further clinical validation, such tools may contribute to scalable oral health monitoring in tele-dentistry workflows, school dental programs, and community health initiatives.

items.abstract: Abstract This study proposes a Foundation Artificial Intelligence (Foundation AI)-based multimodal human–machine interaction framework for an intelligent accelerometer-assisted robotic hand glove to support personalized upper-limb rehabilitation in Parkinson's disease patients. Approximately 150 participants (120 Parkinson's disease patients with Hoehn and Yahr Stage II–III and 30 healthy elderly volunteers) perform six clinically relevant Activities of Daily Living (ADLs), including grasping, eating, drinking, writing, dressing, and opening doors, to capture realistic neuromuscular movement patterns. The lightweight soft robotic glove integrates surface EMG sensors, an IMU incorporating a three-axis accelerometer and gyroscope, flex sensors, force-sensitive resistors, pressure sensors, vibration sensors, and temperature sensors to continuously monitor muscle activity, hand kinematics, tremor characteristics, grip force, wrist orientation, and movement acceleration. The embedded accelerometer enhances movement intention recognition by detecting motion direction, velocity, posture transitions, and dynamic hand activities. To improve accessibility, the framework incorporates three intelligent human–machine interaction modules: voice command control using Whisper and a Bidirectional Transformer for speech-driven robotic assistance; vision-based control via an external webcam, employing MediaPipe Hands for real-time hand landmark detection and Vision Transformer (ViT) for gesture recognition and movement intention estimation; and a mobile healthcare platform supporting personalized rehabilitation, remote monitoring, and secure telemedicine communication through Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), MQTT, and AES-256 encryption. The visual features extracted from the webcam are fused with multimodal physiological and motion signals through a Multimodal Foundation Transformer (MFT) incorporating cross-modal attention and self-supervised contrastive learning to estimate movement intention, tremor severity, hand gesture, finger trajectory, grasp type, and grip force. An Adaptive Impedance Controller subsequently personalizes robotic assistance by regulating actuator torque, finger motion, and wrist orientation in real time while continuously adapting to patient-specific neuromuscular conditions. The proposed framework establishes an intelligent multimodal perception and control architecture for personalized robotic rehabilitation and provides the computational foundation for future Digital Twin-enabled adaptive neuro-rehabilitation.

items.title: Each Reward to Its Relevant Tokens: Reward-Specific Token-Level Credit Assignment for Multi-Reward RL
items.summary: Language models are increasingly trained against several verifiable rewards at once, such as the correctness and the format of a tool call, or the individual constraints of a complex instruction. items.abstract: Language models are increasingly trained against several verifiable rewards at once, such as the correctness and the format of a tool call, or the individual constraints of a complex instruction. Reward-decoupled normalization (GDPO) normalizes each reward separately so that different reward combinations keep distinct advantages, but it still spreads every reward's advantage evenly over the whole response, although each verifier checks only a few positions. We propose MRTPO, which assigns the advantage of each reward to the tokens relevant to it, using the information its verifier checks, without auxiliary models or token-level annotations. For each reward, the policy replays its own response with and without that reward's verifier information, and the per-token Jensen-Shannon distance between the two next-token distributions measures each token's relevance and reassigns the advantage. On text-to-SQL, multi-constraint instruction following and tool calling, MRTPO converges faster and achieves better performance than the compared methods.

items.summary: Large language model agents solve tasks through long sequences of tool calls, and the prevailing design has a single strong model generate every step, although many steps are routine enough for a much smaller model. items.abstract: Large language model agents solve tasks through long sequences of tool calls, and the prevailing design has a single strong model generate every step, although many steps are routine enough for a much smaller model. Existing ways of sharing this work keep the strong model as the generator: routers and collaborative agents decide which model handles each query or step, and speculative methods check a small model's drafts one step at a time, usually against the strong model's own action. We introduce SpecAgent, a collaboration protocol that turns the strong model from the author of each step into a reviewer of steps drafted by a weak model. The weak model executes read-only tool calls as it drafts, so that every step is grounded in real observations, and holds the first action that would modify the environment. The strong model then verifies the drafted segment in a single prefill pass, commits the longest prefix it judges semantically valid, and repairs the first rejected step. Because verification replaces autoregressive decoding with parallel prefill, the strong model decodes only short verdicts and occasional repairs rather than every step. On τ^2-Bench, SpecAgent comes within one point of the strong model's success rate while roughly halving memory traffic and wall time, and on AutomationBench and VitaBench it recovers 44-75% of the quality gap while lowering both. In an edge-cloud deployment on MCP-Atlas with three cloud models, it closes 53-75% of the weak-strong quality gap while the strong model generates at most half as many tokens. These results suggest that a strong model need not author every step of an agent: reviewing grounded drafts retains most of its quality while cutting both latency and memory traffic.

items.abstract: Recent advances in Omni Language Models (OLMs) provide a unified solution for audiovisual video captioning. Nevertheless, existing approaches predominantly treat captioning as an unstructured text generation process, neglecting the inherent semantic structure of videos and leading to suboptimal fine-grained audiovisual alignment. To bridge this gap, we propose EVA-Cap, a novel framework that decomposes captions into atomic audiovisual events and transforms unstructured text supervision into event-centric alignment. We train EVA-Cap via Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on a self-curated dataset, EVA-Data, which is built with event-centric quality control. During the GRPO phase, the model is explicitly optimized against three event-centric alignment targets: global event completeness, intra-event attribution, and inter-event synchronization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EVA-Cap significantly outperforms existing methods in event-centric evaluation (e.g., +9.0% average gain on ChronusAV), while achieving competitive performance on general audiovisual captioning benchmarks (e.g., +3.3% on WorldSense).

items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can elicit specialized visual capabilities in vision-language models (VLMs), yet jointly optimizing heterogeneous objectives often introduces cross-capability gradient conflicts. Training experts independently mitigates this interference, but direct reward optimization may entangle specialized knowledge with reward-hacking biases. This paper proposes Skill-Decoupled On-Policy Expert Distillation (SCOPED), which trains capability-specific experts and extracts explicit skills through reward-guided reflection. During on-policy distillation, these skills guide expert supervision while remaining unavailable to the unified student, encouraging it to internalize procedural knowledge without explicit skills at inference time. Across eight multimodal benchmarks, SCOPED consistently outperforms the backbone and mixed-capability RL, demonstrating the effectiveness of skill-decoupled on-policy expert distillation for integrating independently acquired capabilities. Further analyses reveal interference during joint capability optimization and suggest that skill augmentation promotes more consistent expert trajectories, greater attention to task-relevant visual evidence, and better preservation of specialized expertise in the unified student. All code and data are available at https://github.com/NEUIR/SCOPED.

items.title: Routing Policy Optimization for Online Diffusion Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Reinforcement learning can align visual generators with reward signals beyond their pretraining objectives, but existing score-function methods typically introduce stochasticity by perturbing the reverse denoising trajectory, leading to costly rollout-based optimization. We instead ask whether stochastic exploration can be introduced inside the generator while preserving its original sampler. Routing Policy…
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning can align visual generators with reward signals beyond their pretraining objectives, but existing score-function methods typically introduce stochasticity by perturbing the reverse denoising trajectory, leading to costly rollout-based optimization. We instead ask whether stochastic exploration can be introduced inside the generator while preserving its original sampler. Routing Policy Optimization (RPO) answers this question by turning attention routing into a stochastic exploration action. At a few selected denoising levels, each query block keeps its own block and samples further key blocks in proportion to the generator's native attention mass, or keeps dense attention. The sampled route perturbs the velocity of that transition, and a Gaussian likelihood around the dense velocity scores the perturbation with a score-function objective. RPO further uses a controlled two-rollout estimator: two rollouts share the same prompt, initial latent, routed denoising levels, and dense anchor layers, differing only in their sampled attention routes. Their reward difference provides an advantage signal for the routed transitions. Because the likelihood differentiates the dense velocity itself, the learned updates remain effective after routing is removed. At inference, RPO restores dense attention and retains the original deterministic sampler. Experiments on text-to-image and text-to-video generation show that RPO improves generation quality while achieving nearly 4x higher training efficiency than Flow-GRPO-style methods. Please see our project page at https://velox-world.com/rpo for visual results.

items.abstract: Video world models turn actions and camera motion into long visual rollouts, making video a natural interface for interactive simulation. Such interaction requires responsive generation, yet coherent rollouts must retain visual memory of what has already been generated. Chunked video diffusion models usually keep this context in growing KV caches, so later chunks become progressively slower. To address this bottleneck, we introduce Velox, a training-free attention router for region-level context selection using frustum slab correspondences from streaming geometry. Velox represents historical blocks as camera frustum slabs with depth intervals and obtains current-block depth through recency-priority multiwarp. For well-covered regions, frustum slab overlap softly modulates each layer's model-derived block importance. Uncovered regions retain the model-derived route without geometric bias. The fixed token-block granularity matches FlashAttention-style tiled execution and reduces the attention term that grows with rollout length. Frustum slab construction runs asynchronously with denoising on the same H200. At chunk 48, Velox accelerates attention by 4.36times and denoising by 2.43times. On the full 158-case WBench navigation split, it remains within 0.15 API-free average points of dense LingBot-Fast-Cam. Please see our project page at https://velox-world.com/velox/ for more details.

items.title: Memory as Weights: Internalizing Long-Term History for Streaming Videos
items.summary: Streaming vision-language models (VLMs) must continuously integrate information from the past while remaining responsive to current observations and user queries. Existing memory mechanisms typically compress, retrieve, or cache historical observations and reintroduce them into the input context, forcing historical memory and current observations to compete for limited context. items.abstract: Streaming vision-language models (VLMs) must continuously integrate information from the past while remaining responsive to current observations and user queries. Existing memory mechanisms typically compress, retrieve, or cache historical observations and reintroduce them into the input context, forcing historical memory and current observations to compete for limited context. We propose MaLoW, a streaming memory framework that instead internalizes historical context into evolving lightweight parameter updates. MaLoW uses a recurrent HyperNetwork to incrementally consolidate incoming video observations into fixed-size LoRA weights, allowing historical information to be carried forward without revisiting the full video stream. In doing so, MaLoW represents history as weights, while keeping the current observation as input. To support training, we further construct MaLoW-Instruct, a large-scale streaming video dataset containing 381K question-answer pairs over 56K videos. We conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate that MaLoW achieves strong performance on OVO-Bench, StreamingBench, and StreamArena. On the backward split of OVO-Bench, MaLoW outperforms prior memory approaches by 3.9% to 11.8% across different video backbones while incurring only modest latency overhead. Beyond streaming video understanding, MaLoW also generalizes to vision-language-action models, improving the action success rate on Simpler WidowX by 9.3%.

items.title: A team of Gemini 4 Argon agents beats Minecraft
items.summary: We placed four Gemini 4 Argon agents in a sandboxed Minecraft survival world and gave them one goal: defeat the Ender Dragon. Each agent controlled a player via an open-source library called Mineflayer and coordinated with its teammates through in-game chat and shared memory. No one assigned roles or wrote game logic. The agents planned, wrote, and debugged every program themselves. Researchers could watch the run…
items.abstract: We placed four Gemini 4 Argon agents in a sandboxed Minecraft survival world and gave them one goal: defeat the Ender Dragon. Each agent controlled a player via an open-source library called Mineflayer and coordinated with its teammates through in-game chat and shared memory. No one assigned roles or wrote game logic. The agents planned, wrote, and debugged every program themselves. Researchers could watch the run on a live dashboard and pause or stop it at any time, but they had no cause to intervene. Starting from a randomly generated world on Easy difficulty, the team wrote 2,783 programs and defeated the dragon in 27 hours and 14 minutes, dying 605 times along the way. To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end autonomous completion of Minecraft by AI agents, achieved using only the standard Mineflayer library without pre-scouted seeds or other game-specific tools written by humans. Winning required the agents to keep a coherent plan across thousands of dependent steps for more than a day. Complex real-world software engineering and enterprise tasks demand the same long-horizon coding and multi-agent coordination. We describe the setup, how the run unfolded, the team's strategies (dividing the work, sharing what they learned, recovering each other's items), and the limits of the result.

items.title: Athanor: An Agent-Native System for Autonomous Post-Training Research
items.summary: Recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems build stronger AI systems, is one promising route to superintelligence. We study a weaker form that can be measured today: frontier agents post-training a small raw base model with public data, as a test of their research potential. We build Athanor, an open agent-native system for autonomous post-training research (AutoPostTrain) on real GPUs. We give the agents full…
items.abstract: Recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems build stronger AI systems, is one promising route to superintelligence. We study a weaker form that can be measured today: frontier agents post-training a small raw base model with public data, as a test of their research potential. We build Athanor, an open agent-native system for autonomous post-training research (AutoPostTrain) on real GPUs. We give the agents full research autonomy, low-friction engineering tools, and efficient starter code. The agents carry out the research themselves: they read datasets and evaluation results, build their training data, write and modify training algorithms, tune hyperparameters, and analyze the results to decide what to try next. They work in a sandbox and cannot use external teacher models. Athanor's services supply frozen evaluation, managed jobs, decontaminated data, a persistent research record, and a held-out suite the agents are unaware of. In a 104-hour campaign, a team of four Claude Opus 5.5 agents, each on an eight-GPU node and given no research advice, improves Qwen3-4B-Base from 15.9 to 67.3 on a six-task development suite and from 9.2 to 48.2 on a held-out suite, against 66.5 and 47.9 for the official Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that a team of frontier agents can autonomously post-train a raw base model into a cross-domain generalist model that matches or surpasses the official instruct version on average. The campaign's full record shows that the agents reach this level by recombining known methods and each other's models: SFT on public reasoning data, RL with a rollout change one agent introduced, weight merges across agents, and rounds of self-distillation. With execution handled, today's agents already have the engineering and research ability to conquer this task. We hope Athanor provides a foundation for scaling autonomous AI research.

items.title: 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code
items.summary: We introduce 3DCodeVerse, a research ecosystem that enables coding agents to create editable and verifiable 3D content at scale. 3DCodeVerse comprises large-scale, high-quality datasets of executable 3D code, a coding harness for spatial reasoning and automated verification, and practical guidance for 3D coding. First, we construct 3DCodeVerse-2M, a large-scale curated dataset of standalone 3D executable code. We…
items.abstract: We introduce 3DCodeVerse, a research ecosystem that enables coding agents to create editable and verifiable 3D content at scale. 3DCodeVerse comprises large-scale, high-quality datasets of executable 3D code, a coding harness for spatial reasoning and automated verification, and practical guidance for 3D coding. First, we construct 3DCodeVerse-2M, a large-scale curated dataset of standalone 3D executable code. We build this corpus by collecting open-source data, converting specialized representations, and generating new programs with coding agents. Each program is packaged with the source files and associated assets required for execution in its declared environment, along with available descriptions and verification records. Second, we develop the 3DCodeVerse Harness, a multi-agent directed acyclic graph framework for generating and refining 3D content. It uses execution checks, spatial measurements, and visual feedback to automatically evaluate and revise generated programs without human feedback during generation. Third, we conduct systematic empirical studies of 3D coding, establishing baselines with fine-tuned open models and deriving practical guidance through component-level analyses of our harness. Extensive experiments demonstrate that fine-tuning on our dataset significantly improves the 3D coding capabilities of open-source models. Notably, our 3DCodeVerse harness achieves a 90% win rate against Claude Design (3D Object) in pairwise human evaluations, when both are utilized by Claude Opus 5.5.

items.title: TimeRSI: Towards Self-Improved Agentic Deployment for Time-Series Foundation Models
items.summary: Time-series foundation models provide strong zero-shot forecast, but deployment for real-world applications still requires task-specific designs for model inputs and outputs. Direct inference can leave domain knowledge and recurring forecast errors unaddressed, while tailored pipelines require substantial human expertise and effort. We introduce TimeRSI, a self-improving agentic deployment system around frozen…
items.abstract: Time-series foundation models provide strong zero-shot forecast, but deployment for real-world applications still requires task-specific designs for model inputs and outputs. Direct inference can leave domain knowledge and recurring forecast errors unaddressed, while tailored pipelines require substantial human expertise and effort. We introduce TimeRSI, a self-improving agentic deployment system around frozen forecasting models. A coding agent translates task descriptions into executable pipeline changes. It tests each revision on historical forecasting windows and uses observed errors to guide subsequent revisions. During deployment, an adaptive selector chooses among the resulting pipelines using completed forecasts under similar conditions. Across 198 tasks on TIME and fev-bench, TimeRSI outperforms all submissions on six point and probabilistic forecasting metrics. Controlled comparisons support the value of feedback-guided revision over non-iterative pipeline search. Further experiments verify the generalization with different coding agents and forecasting models. Code is available at https://github.com/haoxin1998/TimeRSI.

items.title: Intern-Decision: Efficient Multimodal Decision Making with Autoregressive Masked Language Modeling
items.summary: Interactive agents repeatedly choose among a finite set of actions, labels, or ordinal outcomes. Generating a free-form response for each choice adds latency and complicates the interface between a model and its environment. We present Intern-Decision, a family of 0.8B, 2B, and 4B multimodal decision models that return structured choices and candidate probabilities from text and optional images. Our autoregressive…
items.abstract: Interactive agents repeatedly choose among a finite set of actions, labels, or ordinal outcomes. Generating a free-form response for each choice adds latency and complicates the interface between a model and its environment. We present Intern-Decision, a family of 0.8B, 2B, and 4B multimodal decision models that return structured choices and candidate probabilities from text and optional images. Our autoregressive masked language modeling objective places one decision placeholder per field in a complete assistant JSON skeleton. Ground-truth symbols appear only in supervision, while all fields are evaluated in a single causal forward pass using the backbone's native language-model head. The 4B model achieves a 90.02% unweighted average accuracy across seven evaluation suites, compared with 88.74% for Jev v1.13.0. For a fixed 289-token request with three fields on one RTX 4090, mean latency is 44.16 ms for the 4B model and approximately 33--34 ms for the smaller models. On a separate 96-case known-distribution pilot, temperature scaling reduces expected multiclass Brier from 0.628 to 0.550 and expected calibration error from 0.213 to 0.089. A confidence-based handoff study on 111 public Jevbench-Hard items improves accuracy from 82/111 (73.87%) to 97/111 (87.39%) by routing 42 items to Atria-Dawn-Preview. We also describe qualitative game, visual interface, and browser demonstrations. These results support compact decision models as a practical component of larger agent systems.

items.title: Terminal-RSI: Recursive Self-Improving Terminal Agents via Recursive Self-Rewrite and Policy-Refine
items.summary: Converting verifier outcomes into useful policy updates and partial progress into complete task resolution is crucial for terminal agents. We present Terminal-RSI, which alternates Recursive Self-Rewrite (RSR) of verified trajectories with critic-inheriting Recursive Policy-Refine (RPR). We formulate Turn-Boundary Skip-Observation GAE (TB-GAE) to retain token-specific baselines while applying decay across…
items.abstract: Converting verifier outcomes into useful policy updates and partial progress into complete task resolution is crucial for terminal agents. We present Terminal-RSI, which alternates Recursive Self-Rewrite (RSR) of verified trajectories with critic-inheriting Recursive Policy-Refine (RPR). We formulate Turn-Boundary Skip-Observation GAE (TB-GAE) to retain token-specific baselines while applying decay across interaction turns. Family Dense Reward (FDR) calibrates semantic progress across task families; Success-Prioritized Reward (SPR) separates strict success from bounded partial credit. A Warm-up Critic Model, recursive critic handoff, and stage-specific learning rates coordinate the two refinement phases. The five-stage sequence from Qwen3.8-27B base model through RSR-1, RPR-1, RSR-2, and RPR-2 yields Terminal-RSI-27B: 19.84% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, 86.52% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 16.95% on Terminal-Bench 3.0, and 79.00% on Terminal-Bench Hard. On LHTB, process reward rises from 0.21 to 0.37 and strict completion from 0/46 to 5/46; SWR100 success doubles from 3.00% to 6.00%. By recursively coupling verified trajectory rewriting with critic-inheriting policy refinement, each retained stage consolidates discovered behaviors and progressively advances the agent from partial local repairs to strict terminal verification.

items.title: SCOPE: Semantic Bounded Credit Optimization for Prompt Engineering in Text-to-image Generation
items.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables language models to improve text-to-image (T2I) generation by rewriting prompts for a frozen image generator. Existing methods typically apply a single signal derived from the image to individual subword tokens, although objects, counts, attributes, and relations form coherent semantic spans. We propose SCOPE, an objective based on Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) that…
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables language models to improve text-to-image (T2I) generation by rewriting prompts for a frozen image generator. Existing methods typically apply a single signal derived from the image to individual subword tokens, although objects, counts, attributes, and relations form coherent semantic spans. We propose SCOPE, an objective based on Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) that aligns update weighting with this structure. The rewriter jointly generates an enhanced prompt and its semantic partition. SCOPE pools shifts in policy log probabilities within each span to derive a shared coefficient for its token losses while retaining a single advantage for each completion. It requires neither separate span rewards nor additional image renders. Across Qwen-Image, SD3, and FLUX.1-dev, SCOPE achieves average relative gains over vanilla GRPO of 9.48% on GeneVal and 7.62% on T2I-CompBench. Ablation studies show that both semantic boundaries and pooling within spans contribute to these gains, supporting semantic structure as a practical inductive bias for prompt engineering with RL.

items.title: AutoSFT: An Agentic System for Automated Data Research in Supervised Fine-Tuning
items.summary: Language model agents increasingly automate post-training, but when given the full training stack they converge on supervised fine-tuning and spend most effort revising training data. Existing systems give the agent one kind of control, selecting rows from a fixed pool or calling a generator, whereas a human data engineer adjusts proportions, prunes, repairs, replaces and synthesizes the data. We design a data…
items.abstract: Language model agents increasingly automate post-training, but when given the full training stack they converge on supervised fine-tuning and spend most effort revising training data. Existing systems give the agent one kind of control, selecting rows from a fixed pool or calling a generator, whereas a human data engineer adjusts proportions, prunes, repairs, replaces and synthesizes the data. We design a data action space for these changes and ask whether an automated system can make the full range rather than one of them, and what structure that requires. We first run this loop with a single agent, and it reaches only one action, adjusting category proportions, while its context fills with execution output and is discarded mid-search. We therefore introduce AutoSFT, a multi-agent system where a meta agent separates execution from analysis, gathers proposals from independent angles, and calls a synthesis subagent for capabilities the pool cannot cover, with the model, the trainer, and the budget fixed within each comparison. Adding each component in turn helps: the executor halves context loss, the analysis subagents lift the best IFEval by +6.5, and synthesis adds +3.4 IFEval and +2.9 IFBench. The same loop transfers to code, where analysis adds +3.7 MBPP+ over a single agent that does not improve. Every result comes from runs that retrain from the base model each round, so each component's effect is individually attributable. Our findings suggest that automating SFT data research depends more on covering diverse data actions than on a stronger single action.

items.title: Speculative Forcing for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation
items.summary: Few-step autoregressive video generators enable streaming generation, yet they run every token through the final denoising step, regardless of how much refinement it needs. We find this uniform computation is often unnecessary: many tokens already closely match their eventual full-step outputs in the initial steps, while others require refinement until the end. We introduce Speculative Forcing, a framework that…
items.abstract: Few-step autoregressive video generators enable streaming generation, yet they run every token through the final denoising step, regardless of how much refinement it needs. We find this uniform computation is often unnecessary: many tokens already closely match their eventual full-step outputs in the initial steps, while others require refinement until the end. We introduce Speculative Forcing, a framework that treats intermediate clean estimates as drafts and predicts when individual tokens can be safely accepted early. Once accepted, a token is frozen as its final output and undergoes no further denoising, while its cached keys and values remain available as context for the remaining tokens. We explore two alternative verifier designs: a training-free one based on similarity to clean content and stability across steps, and a learned one that reads the frozen generator's intermediate features to estimate each token's remaining gap to its full-step output. Across short-video, long-video, and world generation, Speculative Forcing preserves the quality of full-step sampling while substantially reducing computation. On LongLive, it matches the four-step generator with ~1.7 denoising steps per token, running over 1.5x faster at 41.7 and 37.8 fps. On Lingbot-World 2.0, where camera motion continually changes the visible content, it maintains quality with ~2.5 denoising steps per token and runs 1.35x faster at 24.5 fps.

items.title: JevAgentHarness: Benchmarking, Deploying and Training Decision Models That Share Control with LLMs
items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents now fix software, operate computers and serve customers, but their harnesses, the programs that run them, call a large LLM at every step, which makes long tasks slow and costly. Most of these calls end in a multiple-choice decision, such as which tool to call next. Decision models such as Jev answer these questions directly, at a fraction of an LLM call's time and price. We ask how…
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now fix software, operate computers and serve customers, but their harnesses, the programs that run them, call a large LLM at every step, which makes long tasks slow and costly. Most of these calls end in a multiple-choice decision, such as which tool to call next. Decision models such as Jev answer these questions directly, at a fraction of an LLM call's time and price. We ask how a harness can delegate these decisions to a decision model with little loss of success. To evaluate decision models in agentic tasks, we build AgentDecisionBench, which tests them from isolated questions up to control of a running agent, on public benchmarks and our DecisionGym environment. The decision model most accurate on isolated questions solved only 69.5% of agent tasks, and without a fitted confidence threshold, delegating tool choices lowered success by 19.0 points. Building on these findings, we then design JevAgentHarness, which fits this threshold for each choice on the agent's own trajectories and lets the LLM decide below it. Because existing decision models never see the states an agent reaches after its own mistakes, we train AgentDecision-4B, an open 4B model, on such states with Jev's answers as labels. On tasks unlike its training data, the agent solved 91.5% of them with AgentDecision-4B and 82.0% with Jev. On tasks like their training data, 4B models trained this way made agents 81.1-89.0% cheaper and up to 2.5 times faster, without losing 3 or more points of task success. The models, data, and harness will be released at https://github.com/JevAgentHarness/JevAgentHarness.

items.title: SWE-at-Scale: Scalable Issue Synthesis from Historical Bug Fixes
items.summary: As coding agents become increasingly capable, robust evaluation requires a broader and more diverse supply of verifiable software engineering (SWE) tasks. However, real-world tasks are constrained by the natural frequency of issue reporting and the substantial cost of manual curation. Furthermore, existing synthetic approaches rely primarily on the pretrained knowledge of large models coupled with heuristic…
items.abstract: As coding agents become increasingly capable, robust evaluation requires a broader and more diverse supply of verifiable software engineering (SWE) tasks. However, real-world tasks are constrained by the natural frequency of issue reporting and the substantial cost of manual curation. Furthermore, existing synthetic approaches rely primarily on the pretrained knowledge of large models coupled with heuristic prompting, often failing to capture the authentic, complex mechanics of software failures. To exponentially scale SWE task production, we introduce SWE-at-Scale, a framework that automatically synthesizes realistic issues by reverse-engineering real-world software fixes. Our key insight is that historical fixes encapsulate deep mechanistic knowledge of bug formation: inverting a fix transforms repair supervision into bug-induction supervision grounded in actual development scenarios. SWE-at-Scale transfers these learned bug patterns to novel code contexts, repeatedly sampling diverse bug typologies to construct executable SWE tasks. Extensive experiments show that SWE-at-Scale generates more diverse and realistic SWE tasks than current synthesis baselines while posing greater challenges to state-of-the-art coding agents. Notably, SWE-at-Scale can generate distinct bug types from a single code context, with bug diversity scaling robustly even up to 200 generations per file. Overall, SWE-at-Scale turns finite real-world fixes into reusable supervision for scalable synthesis of realistic, diverse, and challenging SWE tasks.
