items.abstract: Abstract Hybrid insulin peptide (HIP) fusion junctions are not encoded in the germline proteome and may be absent during thymic negative selection, allowing microbial mimics to encounter T cells that escaped central tolerance. We present a structure-first screening pipeline for HIP mimics in type 1 diabetes, dataset-scoped negative results for motif yield and backbone RMSD, and ten peptides prioritized for experimental testing. Five reference HIP–TCR–MHC systems guided motif construction. The Swiss-Prot screen targeted ten taxa; a contemporary reconstruction contains reviewed sequences for nine. Of 1,092 motif hits, 55 passed predicted HLA-binding and AlphaFold 3 confidence filters and were modelled with TCRModel2 across five stochastic seeds. A composition-preserving shuffled-proteome control showed no aggregate motif-yield enrichment in the contemporary reconstruction (observed/null ratio 0.97). Candidate backbone RMSD had median 0.315 Å and interquartile range 0.274–0.389 Å; the three controls lay inside the candidate distribution at the 21.8th, 61.8th, and 81.8th percentiles. No single RMSD cutoff perfectly separated these sampled groups. A three-metric native-HIP gate using TCR–pMHC ipTM, interface-pLDDT, and ΔG retained 13 candidates; exclusion of three animal-associated Rotavirus A peptides left ten nominees. The nominated set was unchanged by dropping the redundant Kd criterion but was sensitive to the acceptance thresholds. Supporting comparisons found higher ipTM for 48 of 55 candidates, robust to nonparametric testing and multiple-comparison correction, but the candidate-only AlphaFold 3 pre-filter confounds that separation. RRNVATLQAENVTG from SARS-CoV-2 and SDLLKSVDSEEVRE from human rhinovirus 3 are co-priorities undergoing experimental testing: confidence and directional agreement favor the former, whereas interface energetics favor the latter. Their relative ordering is not statistically established. The pipeline supplies testable peptide–TCR–MHC combinations and documents the limits of motif-yield and backbone-similarity filters in these analyses.

items.abstract: Scientific reasoning moves beyond natural language. The search for a discovery runs across sequences, structures, fields, omics, images and measurements, while language models reason mainly in text. This Perspective sets out four proposals from the Scinetics team. First, we define science tokens: modality-appropriate units of scientific information, spanning native discrete symbols, typed values, continuous representations and learned, decodable codes. A shared interface for these representations would let one model read, write and reason across modalities, so that a chain of science tokens operates on scientifically meaningful states, not on descriptions of them. Second, we define Scientific Super Intelligence (SSI) as a joint crossover: one frozen model that outperforms vertical specialists, such as the AlphaFold series on protein structure prediction, on their own tasks, and outperforms general large language models of the same size on broad scientific reasoning. Capacity, published training precedents, data inventories and compute place the first test of that crossover at 100–300 billion parameters and 10–30 trillion training tokens. Third, we propose ScienceRSI (Science Recursive Self- Improvement) as the route to that window. Following the AI4AI pattern, each larger generation is trained on data that the smaller generation before it produced: the earlier model generates candidate reasoning, screens it and keeps what passes, and in science that screening can be done by a simulation, a database or an experiment. Training this way reduces the dependence on scarce human-written scientific reasoning data and shortens each iteration. Fourth, we propose science-token economics, which separates metered computation from the value of evidence-labelled, reusable scientific assets.

items.abstract: Background Cancer patients face a significantly elevated risk of severe COVID-19 outcomes. Although vaccination is a cornerstone of prevention, data on vaccination coverage and association with survival among Russian cancer patients remain scarce. We assessed COVID-19 vaccination coverage and its association with overall survival in a population-based cohort of cancer patients in Northwest Russia. Methods This retrospective registry-based cohort study integrated data from the Population-Based Cancer Registry (PBCR) of the Arkhangelsk Region and the Nenets Autonomous Okrug, regional vaccination records, and an artificial intelligence (AI)-based analysis of chest computed tomography (CT) scans. The cohort consisted of 1,144 cancer patients who underwent CT between August 2020 and April 2021. Vaccination status was ascertained via data linkage. Overall survival (OS) was compared between vaccinated and unvaccinated patients using Kaplan–Meier analysis and multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression, adjusted for demographic, clinical, and AI-derived CT biomarkers. To mitigate immortal time bias, the primary analysis used a landmark approach restricted to patients alive on March 1, 2021 (N = 1,136). A sensitivity analysis used a November 1, 2021 landmark (N = 894). Vaccination status was defined as receipt of at least one dose before the landmark date. Results Only 6.6% (n=76) of patients received at least one dose of a COVID-19 vaccine (Sputnik V or Sputnik Light). Vaccinated patients were more likely to have earlier-stage cancer and were less likely to be receiving active treatment. In the primary landmark analysis, vaccination was associated with a significantly higher 3-year OS (80.3% vs. 45.7%, p < 0.001). In multivariable analysis, vaccination was independently associated with a 60% lower hazard of all-cause mortality (adjusted HR 0.40, 95% CI 0.25–0.64). AI-detected COVID-19 pneumonia on baseline CT was also an independent predictor of poorer survival (adjusted HR 1.32, 95% CI 1.09–1.59). In the sensitivity analysis (November 1, 2021 landmark), the adjusted HR for vaccination was 0.56 (95% CI 0.34–0.92), showing a consistent but attenuated association. Conclusion This study reveals critically low COVID-19 vaccination coverage among cancer patients in Northwest Russia. Nevertheless, vaccination was strongly associated with a substantial survival benefit, underscoring its importance as a potentially lifesaving intervention for this vulnerable population.

items.abstract: Purpose Existing prognostic models for brain metastases from lung cancer rely on clinical variables and do not capture the biological heterogeneity of host or tumor factors underlying survival outcomes. We evaluated whether MRI-derived radiomic biomarkers improve prognostic stratification beyond clinical variables. We also investigated their biological correlates using matched histopathology. Experimental Design This retrospective study included 103 patients with brain metastases from lung cancer and matched pre-operative MRI and histopathology. Radiomic features from T1-weighted contrast-enhanced and T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences were combined with clinical variables to train Cox proportional hazards, random survival forest, and DeepSurv models for overall survival (OS), CNS progression, and leptomeningeal (LM) progression. Risk groups from an imaging-only model were compared for clinical and histopathologic differences. Results Imaging features improved prognostic performance beyond clinical variables across all modeling frameworks, with the combined clinical-imaging DeepSurv model achieving the highest concordance index for OS (0.728). Risk groups from the best-performing model for each endpoint differed significantly in OS (median 26.7 vs. 9.1 months, p < 0.001) and LM progression ( p = 0.003), but not in CNS progression. Imaging-only risk groups did not differ significantly in any clinical variable, but high-risk patients were less likely to have tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (46% vs. 77%, p = 0.010) and PD-L1 expression ≥ 50% (10% vs. 32%, p = 0.049). Conclusions MRI radiomic biomarkers provide prognostic information beyond established clinical variables in lung cancer brain metastases and correspond to features of the tumor immune microenvironment, supporting their potential to refine risk stratification. Statement of Translational Relevance Brain metastases affect 30-40% of patients with lung cancer. Existing prognostic models rely on clinical variables, which do not fully capture the biological heterogeneity that drives outcomes. We show that machine learning models integrating MRI-derived radiomic features with clinical variables improve prognostic discrimination beyond clinical variables alone. Because these biomarkers are derived from standard-of-care pre-operative imaging, they can be generated without additional testing or delay to treatment planning. Using matched histopathology from resected lesions, we further show that imaging-defined risk groups do not simply reproduce established clinical risk factors but instead correspond to differences in the tumor immune microenvironment, including tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and PD-L1 expression. These findings support the use of quantitative imaging biomarkers as a non-invasive method to refine risk stratification at diagnosis, informing treatment selection and clinical trial enrollment for patients with brain metastases from lung cancer.

items.abstract: Background: Genetic conditions are common in congenital heart disease (CHD) and affect care, but are often missed or diagnosed late. We asked whether routine clinical data can shortlist the most likely genetic conditions. Methods: Retrospective single-center cohort of children with CHD and an echocardiogram who had either a confirmed genetic diagnosis or negative cytogenetic testing and CHD gene sequencing. Echocardiogram images and serial medical record data were added as model inputs in the order they become clinically available. Class balanced logistic regression (LR) and a multimodal deep learning fusion network were fitted to the same inputs at each step. The primary metric was balanced top-3 accuracy (correct diagnosis among the top three, averaged across conditions), with bootstrap intervals. Results: The cohort included 1,720 children (988 with common CHD-associated genetic conditions, 231 rare diagnoses, 501 negative testing). Using only inputs generated at the echocardiogram visit, LR reached a balanced top-3 accuracy 0.758 (chance 0.429). Serial records, radiology notes and ICD-10 codes, raised this to 0.809. Multimodal fusion performed similarly at each stage. With a genetic condition withheld from training, the fusion embedding placed affected children nearest to others sharing a gene group in 0.37 of cases versus 0.10 without the embedding (+0.268 [95% CI +0.242, +0.295]). Conclusions: Routine clinical data available at first echocardiogram can help identify likely genetic diagnoses, and later coded inputs ceiling. Multimodal fusion added no accuracy over LR, but places children sharing a genetic cause near one another, making nearest-neighbor retrieval informative for undiagnosed children.

items.abstract: Multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) assays such as ImmunoProfile provide standardized quantification of prognostic immune markers but are costly and not routinely used in clinical settings. We developed a weakly-supervised AI model, HistoProfile, to estimate intratumoral cell densities of key immune biomarkers (CD8, FOXP3, PD-1, and PD-L1) and the PD-L1 tumor proportion score from routine H&E-stained whole-slide images. Trained on a large pan-cancer cohort with paired H&E and mIF data, HistoProfile discriminated biomarker-high from biomarker-low tumors in held-out samples and tumor-specific subgroups (AUROCs of 0.78-0.89 across biomarkers). Critically, the estimated biomarkers preserved prognostic stratification in downstream survival analyses, and showed cancer-specific survival associations across TCGA cohorts where mIF is unavailable. These findings support scalable H&E-based estimation of key immune biomarker measurements for large-scale immune profiling and risk stratification.

items.summary: Single-cell foundation models typically represent cells as flat sequences of individual genes, requiring higher-order biological organization to be inferred implicitly from sparse expression profiles. items.abstract: Single-cell foundation models typically represent cells as flat sequences of individual genes, requiring higher-order biological organization to be inferred implicitly from sparse expression profiles. Similar to the evolution from character-level to semantic tokenization in natural language processing,we hypothesize that cellular states can be more efficiently represented using biologically meaningful intermediate units. Here we present BioMod, a 50-million-parameter single-cell foundation model that introduces biological modules as representation units between genes and cells. BioMod constructs an overlapping vocabulary of 660 biological modules derived from curated pathways and data-driven gene programs, replacing thousands of gene-level inputs with compact module representations. Pretrained on approximately 73 million human cells using high-ratio module masking with an asymmetric decoder, BioMod achieves state-of-the-art performance across cell-type annotation, zero-shot batch integration, perturbation-response prediction and drug-response forecasting while maintaining a compact architecture that enables efficient inference on a single GPU. Module-level analyses further demonstrate that BioMod captures biologically meaningful cellular programs and preserves pathway-level organization.

items.abstract: Purpose Cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 inhibitors in combination with endocrine therapy have become widely adopted as a first-line treatment approach for hormone receptor-positive (HR+)/human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative (HER2−) advanced breast cancer (ABC). Through a collaboration between Novartis and the US Food and Drug Administration, we integrated multimodal data from phase III MONALEESA trials to identify novel prognostic factors for HR+/HER2−ABC. Experimental Design Baseline clinical and genomics data were collected from patients in the MONALEESA-2, −3, and −7 trials. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) from plasma samples and gene expression in archival tumor biopsies were analyzed. Machine learning models were trained ( n = 1,355) on progression-free survival (PFS) using multimodal features via fusion models. In a test set ( n = 382), prognostic performances were evaluated using the Kaplan-Meier, Cox, and Weibull models. Results The late fusion model achieved a prognostic performance (C-index: 0.727, 95% CI: 0.641–0.799) slightly outperforming early fusion (C-index: 0.718, 95% CI: 0.631–0.791) and single-modality models. Model-based risk stratification identified distinct low- and high-risk groups (PFS HR, 0.28; 95% CI: 0.20–0.38). Among the top 40 features for progression risk (18 clinical, 20 gene expression, and 2 ctDNA), these were associated with higher risk: liver involvement, higher histological grades, early relapse; lower STC2 and RBBP8 expressions and higher FBX05 expression; and higher tumor mutational burden and ctDNA purity. Conclusions Integrating clinical and genomic modalities improved progression risk prediction compared with single-modality models, while highlighting salient features that inform the underlying biology and support hypothesis generation.

items.abstract: Abstract Monogenic diabetes is caused by pathogenic variants in genes involved in pancreatic development, β-cell function, and glucose homeostasis, yet a substantial proportion of variants identified through genetic testing are classified as Variants of Uncertain Significance (VUS) due to insufficient or conflicting evidence. An explainable machine learning pipeline was developed to prioritize VUS across 22 established monogenic diabetes genes. Confidently classified pathogenic and benign single nucleotide variants (SNVs) were curated from ClinVar (GRCh38, germline, review status ≥1 star) and annotated with consequence, functional-prediction, conservation, and population-frequency features via the Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor (VEP) REST API and MyVariant.info (dbNSFP). Four classifiers (logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, LightGBM) were compared via stratified cross-validation; all achieved area under the precision–recall curve (AUPRC) of 0.987–0.989, with logistic regression selected for its interpretability. On a held-out test set (n=771), the model achieved ROC-AUC = 0.9989 and AUPRC = 0.9970, with recall of 1.00 on the pathogenic class. Systematic feature ablation revealed that reported performance is substantially inflated by structural overlap between the feature set and American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) criteria used to originally classify ClinVar variants (PP3/BP4-only features: accuracy 0.953; consequence-and-frequency-only: 0.911), a circularity phenomenon previously documented for this class of model. Restricting evaluation to non-missense variants, where computational-evidence criteria could not have been directly invoked by curators, the model still substantially outperformed a majority-class baseline (99.0% vs. 87.0%), indicating genuine discriminative signal beyond simple reconstruction of curator logic. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis identified CADD score, gnomAD allele frequency, and PolyPhen score as the strongest global predictors, with directionality consistent with established variant biology throughout. The trained model was applied to 6,306 VUS across these genes, producing a ranked, per-variant-explained prioritization list intended to support, not replace, expert clinical review. This work is framed explicitly as an interpretable evidence-integration and triage tool for a defined gene set, rather than as a novel independent pathogenicity discriminator, and the full pipeline, from raw ClinVar records to the final ranked output, is openly documented for reuse.

items.abstract: Microfluidics has emerged as an important platform for manipulating and analyzing small volumes of fluids, cells, biomolecules, and particles with high precision. Its ability to control microscale flows and integrate multiple analytical steps has enabled diverse biomedical technologies, including lab-on-a-chip, point-of-care diagnostics, organ-on-chip, and microphysiological systems. This review summarizes the fundamental principles of biomedical microfluidics, including microscale fluid dynamics, laminar flow, diffusion, and key dimensionless parameters, together with major platform formats such as continuous-flow, droplet-based, and digital microfluidics. Recent fabrication approaches, including photolithography, soft lithography, molding, laser-based methods, 3D printing, micromilling, and paper- and lamination-based techniques, are also discussed. The review highlights applications in cancer and liquid biopsy, infectious disease diagnostics, cardiovascular and neurological disorders, organ-on-chip models, drug screening and toxicity testing, pharmaceutical synthesis, drug delivery, single-cell analysis, and regenerative and reproductive medicine. Particular attention is given to the growing use of microfluidics for personalized and human-relevant biomedical research. The review further examines the major challenges associated with microfluidic biomedical systems, including fabrication reproducibility, material compatibility, biological complexity, standardization, scalability and manufacturing, clinical validation, regulatory requirements, and integration with advanced computational approaches such as artificial intelligence and machine learning. Finally, future perspectives are discussed, with particular emphasis on personalized medicine, decentralized diagnostics, human-relevant drug development, multi-organ microphysiological systems, wearable and implantable microfluidics, and automated biomedical platforms.

items.summary: Language-model agents sometimes act beyond their authorization and then misreport what they did. On CAPE-Bench, matched agent tasks in which one fact decides whether an action is authorized, frontier open-weight agents do both, and one behavior marks the lie: retroactive permission laundering, acting and then asking permission as if the action were pending, precedes a false report in 70% of 1081 fresh informed…
items.abstract: Language-model agents sometimes act beyond their authorization and then misreport what they did. On CAPE-Bench, matched agent tasks in which one fact decides whether an action is authorized, frontier open-weight agents do both, and one behavior marks the lie: retroactive permission laundering, acting and then asking permission as if the action were pending, precedes a false report in 70% of 1081 fresh informed violations, against 8% otherwise (preregistered odds ratio 7.0); frontier agents on tau^2-bench instead fabricate the authorization before violating. A linear readout of the agent's residual stream forecasts the violation before the action (AUROC 0.94) and the false report before the report, and beats chain-of-thought monitors when the agent is pressured to hide its reasoning. Gating every proposed action on this forecast cuts violations over whole episodes in four model families, and sending repeated flags to an approver keeps authorized work (Gemma-4: violations 0.70 -> 0.09, completion 1.00; a model approver that escalates unclear cases keeps this gain with a person seeing 25% of asks), at about 10-8 of the agent's compute and 109 times less than a chain-of-thought monitor. On AgentDojo, an external prompt-injection benchmark, the same readout calibrated on 29 tasks, with the steering unchanged, cuts attack success on unseen tasks in two families (Gemma-4 11.7% -> 5.7%, gpt-oss 28.5% -> 17.5%) while keeping benign utility (Gemma-4 0.637 vs 0.637; gpt-oss 0.667 vs 0.681). Preventing the violation is also the most reliable way to prevent the lie (misreported violations 0.10 -> 0.01 pooled over three families, preregistered), whereas lie-specific fixes after a violation are weak. All tests are preregistered and hash-locked; code, data and the full record, including tests that did not pass, are at https://github.com/AryaFayyazi/Honesty.

items.abstract: Latent diffusion models generate images as codes of an image tokenizer, whose decoder turns them into the pixel image. Recent tokenizers improve how well these codes reconstruct an image and how easily a generator learns them. Yet a generator does not reproduce the codes of training images, and when a generated code lands outside what the decoder expects, the decoded image contains imperfections. Current methods make the decoder more robust to generated codes by adding noise during training. However, generated codes lie between the training codes and resemble their mixture more than one of them plus noise. To improve generated images, decoders should therefore be trained on codes in the space between training samples. We propose InterpTok, which fine-tunes MAETok to decode mixtures of image codes into natural images. Since no target image exists between two training samples, a discriminator judges whether each decoded mixture looks as natural as its two sources. A mixing ratio loss requires the decoded mixture to keep the mixing ratio of the two codes. Together, they prevent collapse to a trivial solution and yield a sharp and natural composition of both images. InterpTok keeps MAETok's reconstruction quality and improves interpolation quality more than threefold, the best of all tokenizers in a recent benchmark. Beyond interpolation, InterpTok improves the generation FID of a matched diffusion transformer from 11.61 to 8.48 without guidance, and even reaches 8.11 at an eighth of the sampling steps, where the generator on MAETok's codes worsens. The generator trained on our tokenizer also reaches the final result of the one trained on MAETok at half the training steps. Our findings show that the space between image codes can and should be explicitly supervised rather than ignored.

items.summary: Video-based interactive world models aim to enable real-time, user-controllable environments. Yet most existing systems are trained and rolled out at a fixed temporal rate, limiting both runtime-rate adaptation and physical-horizon coverage -- a limitation we term temporal-rate coupling. items.abstract: Video-based interactive world models aim to enable real-time, user-controllable environments. Yet most existing systems are trained and rolled out at a fixed temporal rate, limiting both runtime-rate adaptation and physical-horizon coverage -- a limitation we term temporal-rate coupling. Specifically, when runtime generation throughput differs from the learned temporal rate, the generated world evolves unintentionally more slowly or quickly. Moreover, using a single temporal rate imposes an inherent trade-off between temporal granularity and physical horizon: higher rates capture finer motion but cover a shorter duration under a fixed context window. To address both limitations, we introduce Rate-Adaptive Rollout (RAR), a framework that enables interactive world models to roll out at controllable temporal rates. At its core, Stride-RoPE aligns latent frames sampled at different rates on a shared physical-time coordinate, enabling consistent multi-rate rollout, unseen-rate generalization, and online rate switching without discarding history. Meanwhile, RAR uses multi-stride video sampling to enable joint learning of fine-grained dynamics and long-horizon evolution. Across action- and camera-controlled environments, RAR achieves temporally consistent multi-rate rollout and online rate switching while preserving high-rate generation quality and extending physical horizons under matched training budgets. RAR also transfers to pretrained world models while preserving perceptual quality.

items.summary: LLM-based multi-agent collaboration is increasingly used to solve complex tasks by dividing work among specialized agents and integrating complementary expertise. items.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent collaboration is increasingly used to solve complex tasks by dividing work among specialized agents and integrating complementary expertise. Yet existing systems and evaluations largely rest on an implicit perfect-colleague assumption: collaborators provide correct and complete information and respond promptly to requests. In realistic teamwork, however, collaborators may return information that does not answer the intended question, provide insufficient detail to support a decision, or fail to respond to a request. To separate task-solving competence from the ability to recover an unreliable evidence-gathering process, we introduce the Unreliable Colleagues Benchmark (UnCoBench), which organizes behavioral failures through Misaligned, Incomplete, and Missed settings. The main agent need to verify contextual correctness, diagnose information gap and track unresolved dependencies in order to obtain the correct evidence for solving the task. We also introduce a verifiable and scalable automated generation pipeline that pairs LLM-based scenario generation with executable checks of answer uniqueness and role necessity. Results across ten models show that similar reliable-setting performance can result in different robustness to unreliable evidence. Trace analysis reveals frequent omissions of corrective follow-up, and the recovery behavior involves inefficient waiting and redundant queries. These findings show that robust collaboration requires not only sound reasoning, but also targeted action to diagnose evidence failures, recover relevant information, and integrate it into decisions. Our data and source code are available at https://github.com/iNLP-Lab/UnCoBench.

items.title: TPPO: Tracking-Value PPO For Language Model Reasoning

items.abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) is widely used in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for language-model reasoning. While value evolution along trajectory characterizes relative token-level credit, yet standard critics often fail to track it under sparse terminal rewards. To model this evolution, we analyze the relation between successive prefix values and show that they admit a Bayesian decomposition with additive updates in log-odds space. We use this additive structure to construct Tracking-Value PPO (\method), a cumulative value parameterization that sums position-wise scalar outputs into value logits. These outputs are learned through terminal-outcome supervision on the reconstructed values. \method improves aggregate mathematical reasoning scores over PPO by 7.0 and 8.4 points on Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively, while improving out-of-distribution generalization. Gains extend to Qwen3-4B, Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, Qwen3.5-9B and to countdown, and scientific coding tasks. Further analysis shows more accurate tracking of value evolution and more reliable advantage estimates. Our code is publicly available in https://github.com/LINs-lab/TPPO.

items.title: Spectral-Driven Adaptive-Rank Optimizer for Large Language Model Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards

items.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is reshaping how large language models (LLMs) acquire reasoning capabilities, yet the optimizers used remain largely inherited from teacher-forcing training. This raises a fundamental question: does RLVR induce a distinct optimization geometry that calls for a different optimizer? We investigate this question through the spectral structure of LLM gradients and find that gradient energy progressively concentrates into a shrinking effective subspace, which is characteristic of RLVR, as it is absent under supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and is largely removed when the verifiable reward is replaced by a random one. Moreover, the rank required to capture a fixed fraction of gradient energy steadily decreases over training, revealing that the effective dimensionality of useful updates itself evolves with training. These findings motivate a new optimization principle: rather than prescribing the update rank externally, an optimizer should adapt its rank to the evolving spectral structure of the gradient. We introduce Ares (Adaptive Rank-Effective Spectral Optimization), which estimates the effective update rank from the gradient's spectral energy distribution, tracks its evolution, and confines the gradient signal driving each update to the resulting low-rank subspace. Across LLMs of different scales, Ares improves accuracy over widely used optimizers and generalizes across RLVR algorithms and tasks. Results suggest that effective optimization may require optimizers to be designed around the geometry and dynamics of the training process. We release the code and data at https://github.com/RUCAIBox/Ares.

items.title: AReA: Adaptive Receptive-Field Attention for Efficient High-Resolution Diffusion Transformers
items.summary: Generating images beyond the training resolution of Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) remains challenging, as the number of tokens grows rapidly with resolution, full attention becomes expensive, and outputs often suffer from structural distortions and degraded detail. We identify uniform full attention as the common source of both problems. Attending to all tokens at every step causes quadratic cost and exposes the…
items.abstract: Generating images beyond the training resolution of Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) remains challenging, as the number of tokens grows rapidly with resolution, full attention becomes expensive, and outputs often suffer from structural distortions and degraded detail. We identify uniform full attention as the common source of both problems. Attending to all tokens at every step causes quadratic cost and exposes the model to more tokens and relative distances beyond the training range, pushing the model out of distribution. We observe that attention's effective receptive field narrows during denoising, from global in early steps that form structure to local in later steps that refine details. We propose AReA, a training-free attention mechanism whose receptive field evolves from coarse to fine, following the denoising progression. In early steps, AReA applies cross-scale coarse attention over downsampled keys and values, capturing global context, while in later steps it applies local attention within progressively shrinking windows. Without additional parameters or training, experiments show that AReA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art training-free baselines across target resolutions and different models, while also being faster and more efficient.

items.summary: Chest X-ray (CXR) interpretation often requires integrating visual findings with task-specific evidence rather than relying on direct visual recognition alone. items.abstract: Chest X-ray (CXR) interpretation often requires integrating visual findings with task-specific evidence rather than relying on direct visual recognition alone. While tool-augmented medical agents can supply such evidence via external modules, they often lack explicit mechanisms for learning when auxiliary evidence is needed and for preventing inapplicable quantitative evidence from entering diagnostic reasoning. To address this, we propose X-Ragent, a post-training framework for tool-augmented reinforcement learning that decouples learned auxiliary-evidence seeking from validity-gated quantitative measurement acquisition for evidence-grounded CXR reasoning. We construct Rad-CoT, a 7.7K-sample corpus combining causally ordered tool-augmented trajectories with report-style diagnostic reasoning, and use it to initialize Qwen3-VL-8B via agentic supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We then optimize the policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using an accuracy-gated reward that applies process-level terms for measurement consistency and auxiliary-tool cost only to correct trajectories, preventing plausible process behavior from compensating for an incorrect diagnosis. Across three CXR benchmarks, X-Ragent achieves the strongest results, including an 8.6-point improvement on the fully held-out ChestAgentBench. By seeking evidence selectively and admitting only valid measurements, X-Ragent supports more faithful and evidence-grounded CXR reasoning.

items.title: Elephant in the Fridge: Constant-Memory Frame Packing for Long Video Understanding
items.summary: Hour-long videos, streaming feeds, and movie-length content are pushing vision-language models (VLMs) past their breaking point -- the standard recipe of encoding each frame into visual tokens yields sequences that grow linearly with video length, causing prohibitive memory consumption and inference latency. items.abstract: Hour-long videos, streaming feeds, and movie-length content are pushing vision-language models (VLMs) past their breaking point -- the standard recipe of encoding each frame into visual tokens yields sequences that grow linearly with video length, causing prohibitive memory consumption and inference latency. Existing approaches, such as token reduction and keyframe selection, shorten the token sequence but leave the O(n) scaling intact, failing to resolve the fundamental bottleneck. We propose FramePack-U, a strikingly simple, training-free frame packing framework that compresses arbitrarily long videos into a fixed size visual representation at constant memory cost. FramePack-U requires no fine-tuning or architectural modification -- it plugs directly into off-the-shelf VLMs at inference time. Inspired by FramePack from the generation literature, we propose a content-aware compression strategy for visual understanding under a fixed token budget. Specifically, FramePack-U (1) scores each frame by its semantic similarity to the text prompt and ranks frames in a diversity-driven manner, and (2) packs the selected frames at varying resolutions into a fixed-length context window. This concentrates the memory budget on frames that are both instruction-relevant and visually diverse. While FramePack-U can in theory pack arbitrarily many frames into the fixed budget, we identify an empirical instantiation that generalizes robustly across settings. Extensive experiments on LongVideoBench, MLVU, and Video-MME show that FramePack-U consistently outperforms full-resolution baselines and prior token reduction and keyframe selection methods across diverse model families, parameter scales, and frame budgets. Notably, on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with a 128-frame budget, FramePack-U yields gains of +12.9\%, +10.6\%, and +9.7\% over the official model on the three benchmarks, respectively.

items.title: CineRecon: Benchmarking Frontier Models for Agentic Cinematic Reconstruction
items.summary: Reconstructing reference videos as editable dynamic 3D scenes is an important path toward controllable video generation for filmmaking: these scenes provide modifiable, renderable visual proxies that enable explicit control over scene layout, subject actions, and camera behavior. items.abstract: Reconstructing reference videos as editable dynamic 3D scenes is an important path toward controllable video generation for filmmaking: these scenes provide modifiable, renderable visual proxies that enable explicit control over scene layout, subject actions, and camera behavior. To evaluate agents' ability to reconstruct editable dynamic 3D scenes from dynamic reference videos, we introduce CineRecon, a benchmark comprising 50 reference videos and 360 annotated evaluation clips. The reference videos span film, real-world footage, and games. Given a complete video, an agent uses tools to construct, animate, render, and refine its reconstruction. We evaluate this task under three representation settings: Proxy, Simplified, and Detailed. These settings increase geometric and appearance requirements while retaining the same requirements for spatial relations, camera behavior, and subject dynamics. This design tests whether agents can reproduce the events in a video when detailed appearance is unnecessary, and how performance changes as representation requirements increase. For evaluation, we construct checklists that associate observable properties and events with specific entities and times. A vision-language judge compares timestamp-aligned reference and rendered frames across 11 categories, grouped into camera, static, and dynamic consistency dimensions. We evaluate 12 models using their corresponding agent harnesses and find failures across all three dimensions. Subject motions and interactions remain difficult to reproduce even under the Proxy setting.

items.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) extend LLMs to process heterogeneous modalities (e.g., vision, audio, and IMU signals) alongside language, enabling a broader range of multimodal tasks. Yet we find that these models often fail to express information from non-textual modalities even when they perceive it correctly. We term this disconnect knows-but-cannot-say. To investigate this phenomenon, we introduce Token-level Modality Alignment (TMA), which measures the alignment between individual modality representations and response representations. Our analysis shows that non-textual representations are less aligned with response tokens and receive less attention than textual representations, suggesting a potential explanation for uneven modality preferences. Motivated by these findings, we propose OmniCatalyst, a simple perceive rightarrow infer strategy that complements the original modality inputs with self-generated text, making non-textual knowledge more accessible. Across seven Omni-LLMs, OmniCatalyst consistently improves performance (+7.29%) and yields more balanced modality preferences, with further gains from diverse training strategies. Further analysis demonstrates that the knowledge extraction phases increase TMA, suggesting that improved alignment makes non-textual information more accessible during response generation. In summary, our findings uncover how Omni-LLMs can better express modality knowledge through language. Our code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/OmniLLM.

items.title: InfoVis: Unified Slide Image Generation and Editing
items.summary: Generating and editing presentation slides requires models to combine accurate text rendering, instruction following, visual grounding, aesthetic design, and precise editing within one canvas. Existing work covers only subsets of these capabilities and lacks large-scale slide-native supervision and diagnostic evaluation. We formulate four slide-centric tasks and build a scalable data engine with over 13M…
items.abstract: Generating and editing presentation slides requires models to combine accurate text rendering, instruction following, visual grounding, aesthetic design, and precise editing within one canvas. Existing work covers only subsets of these capabilities and lacks large-scale slide-native supervision and diagnostic evaluation. We formulate four slide-centric tasks and build a scalable data engine with over 13M continual-pretraining records and 1.9M supervised fine-tuning records. We also introduce VisSlideBench, a benchmark of 1,527 manually screened instances that covers all four tasks with task-specific, multidimensional evaluation. Its automatic rankings agree with blinded, dimension-wise human rankings. Using these resources, we train InfoVis, a unified 9B slide generation and editing model. On VisSlideBench, InfoVis leads every evaluated open-source model on all eleven metrics and scores 7.94 overall against 7.99 for Nano-Banana-2. Starting from FLUX.2-klein-base-9B, slide-specific post-training adds 1.6 points overall, with the largest generation gains in content faithfulness; the remaining gap to proprietary models is smallest in content faithfulness and largest in aesthetic quality. Built on InfoVis, our document-to-slide workflow achieves the second-highest Aesthetics score on the external SlidesGen-Bench. We will release the model, code, data, and benchmark.

items.title: Calibrated Typed Decisions for Entity, Relation, and Event Extraction
items.summary: Information extraction models often perform well on the datasets they are trained on, but transferring to new domains and annotation guidelines remains challenging. Supporting user-specified types alone does not resolve this problem. We present CalOn, a unified 0.6B-parameter encoder for entity, relation, and event extraction across datasets and schemas. The model jointly encodes text and type definitions, then…
items.abstract: Information extraction models often perform well on the datasets they are trained on, but transferring to new domains and annotation guidelines remains challenging. Supporting user-specified types alone does not resolve this problem. We present CalOn, a unified 0.6B-parameter encoder for entity, relation, and event extraction across datasets and schemas. The model jointly encodes text and type definitions, then directly identifies entity spans, relations between spans, and event triggers and arguments. Its extraction decisions consider the requested types together, using their combined evidence to identify relevant candidates before assigning a type. This gives all three tasks a common probabilistic formulation while keeping every extracted mention anchored to the input text. We train on diverse sources, and supplement supervised learning with a reward that encourages correct extractions and penalises incorrect ones. Across 40 benchmarks, CalOn outperforms the evaluated baselines on most benchmarks. It leads all reported relation extraction benchmarks and achieves the highest average F1 for event triggers and arguments with gold triggers. The same model also performs strongly on aspect sentiment triplet extraction and pronoun resolution through its span-pair formulation. A correction for the probability bias introduced during training improves confidence estimates for entities, relations, and event arguments after calibration, with little change in F1.

items.title: FreeSolo: Linear-time Sparse Attention with Zero-Shot Length Extrapolation
items.summary: Linear-time sequence models typically store long-context information in a recurrent state. A fixed-size state limits how much information can be stored, while hybrid architectures that add full attention for better recall incur quadratic sequence cost. Alternatively, sparse attention with continued pretraining (CPT) can extend the effective context length. Generalization beyond the trained length remains…
items.abstract: Linear-time sequence models typically store long-context information in a recurrent state. A fixed-size state limits how much information can be stored, while hybrid architectures that add full attention for better recall incur quadratic sequence cost. Alternatively, sparse attention with continued pretraining (CPT) can extend the effective context length. Generalization beyond the trained length remains challenging, however, and CPT can be costly. We introduce FreeSolo, a native sparse attention mechanism with a short-range sliding window branch and a long-range branch that selects keypoint cells for direct token attention. Its linear-time variant, FS-L, learns to prune the prefix before query-dependent selection through short CPT. FS-B searches balanced trees with O(Nlog^2 N) algorithmic cost including radix-sort construction. FreeSolo demonstrates better zero-shot length extrapolation than the baselines without long-context fine-tuning.

items.abstract: Can a vision-language model tell left from right? Modern VLMs solve visual puzzles and follow hour-long videos, yet when asked whether the camera moved left or right, most do no better than a coin flip. Adding camera-motion data or geometric representations has been tried, separately, and neither closes the gap. We argue that camera-motion understanding needs two conditions at once: the representation must couple off-screen camera motion with on-screen flow dynamics, and it must be interpreted by the language model rather than trained as a standalone pose or depth estimator. We propose CameraVLM, which pairs a motion-state representation with state-language alignment. Camera tokens capture how the camera moves off screen, flow tokens capture how the subject and background move on screen, and a two-stage training strategy keeps language in the loop so that both are learned together with camera-motion semantics. With only 9B parameters, CameraVLM outperforms all open-source and camera-motion-specific models by a wide margin across three benchmarks and more than 20 baselines, and matches or surpasses GPT-6 Astra as well as human viewers in a 48-participant study. Project page: https://3dagentworld.github.io/CameraVLM/

items.abstract: We study environment scaling as a way to increase agent-benchmark difficulty while holding core task objectives fixed. Our framework, Recursive Environment Scaling (RES), transforms existing benchmark environments while preserving their objectives and completion requirements. A proposer changes information access, resource relations, and execution dependencies; execution-grounded checks validate the resulting candidate, and accepted changes are inherited across rounds. This produces related environments for paired evaluation and training-trajectory collection. Experiments on 294 initial tasks from three benchmarks show lower task success for all six evaluation models, with decreases of 57.14--77.14 percentage points on Claw-Eval-Live. With equal trajectory counts and identical optimization settings, fine-tuning on RES trajectories outperforms original-trajectory SFT in all nine model--benchmark comparisons by 7.00--14.61 percentage points. Ablations identify recursive inheritance and dependency composition as important contributors to increased difficulty. Together, these results support environment scaling for both agent evaluation and training.

items.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically uses small rollout groups per prompt, where repeated sampling from the same policy can yield highly similar trajectories, reducing within-group reward variation and weakening group-relative advantage signals. items.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically uses small rollout groups per prompt, where repeated sampling from the same policy can yield highly similar trajectories, reducing within-group reward variation and weakening group-relative advantage signals. Existing remedies such as higher sampling temperature, entropy bonuses, asymmetric clipping, and larger rollout budgets broaden sampling or modify policy updates but leave rollout conditioning unchanged. In this paper, we propose EDEN (Embedding-space Directional Exploration via anchored Noise), which intervenes at the rollout source through anchored input perturbations. EDEN explores beyond the policy's own rollouts. Within the same rollout budget, it replaces a small fraction of standard rollouts in each group with rollouts that the same policy generates from the prompt plus a single appended, perturbed embedding position, rather than from the prompt alone. Gaussian noise drives variation, while a shared anchor provides a common conditioning direction within each prompt group. Selected perturbed rollouts contribute to GRPO updates with downweighted advantages, and the model architecture, discrete decoding, and test-time inference remain unchanged. Across model scales and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, EDEN outperforms GRPO and the exploration controls evaluated in the same pipeline, with the largest gains in sampled solution coverage. Analyses show that more prompt groups provide non-zero group-relative learning signals and that noise and anchoring play complementary roles. Intervening at the rollout source is thus an effective lever for exploration in RLVR.

items.title: PINT: A Unified Model with Shared Predictive Intent for Robot Manipulation
items.summary: Generalist robot manipulation can benefit from pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) for semantic reasoning and video generation models (VGMs) for world modeling. However, existing unified models that directly fuse them through shared attention at multiple layers can make it harder to draw on their specialized capabilities. items.abstract: Generalist robot manipulation can benefit from pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) for semantic reasoning and video generation models (VGMs) for world modeling. However, existing unified models that directly fuse them through shared attention at multiple layers can make it harder to draw on their specialized capabilities. We introduce PINT, a unified model that coordinates semantic reasoning, world modeling, and action generation through a shared chunk-level Predictive Intent while preserving expert-specific pathways. PINT inserts learnable Intent Tokens into the VLM sequence to form this representation, conditioning both the VGM and an Action Expert (AE). It replaces only the VGM's prompt conditioning and retains the VGM at inference, where the AE reads its representations through one-way attention. Rather than prescribing what Predictive Intent should encode, PINT learns it jointly from the native prediction objectives of the VLM, VGM, and AE, which provide complementary views of the same upcoming task execution. Training uses two stages: Stage 1 freezes the VGM so that future video prediction shapes Predictive Intent with task-relevant future dynamics, while Stage 2 fixes the learned Intent and adapts the VGM and AE. Without embodied pretraining, PINT achieves strong in-distribution (ID) performance and substantially improves out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, reaching 15.5% on RoboTwin 2.0-Hard compared with 1.8% for Fast-WAM and 3.2% for StarVLA, and 79.5% on LIBERO-Plus compared with 51.5% and 75.0%, respectively. Across five real-world bimanual tasks, PINT reaches 68% ID and 24% OOD success, compared with 35%/9% for pretrained Motus and 67%/35% for pretrained π_{0.5}.

items.summary: Catalytic metal-binding sites are established drug targets for many human diseases, yet systematic study of how metal function relates to disease is limited by the lack of a resource combining structural localization of human metal-binding sites with catalytic annotation at scale. We introduce HEAM (the Human Enzymatic Annotation of Metalloproteins), a structurally annotated dataset of 1,933 human metalloenzymes and…
items.abstract: Catalytic metal-binding sites are established drug targets for many human diseases, yet systematic study of how metal function relates to disease is limited by the lack of a resource combining structural localization of human metal-binding sites with catalytic annotation at scale. We introduce HEAM (the Human Enzymatic Annotation of Metalloproteins), a structurally annotated dataset of 1,933 human metalloenzymes and 1,171 non-catalytic metalloproteins. HEAM incorporates annotated metals into protein structures at their corresponding binding sites and classifies each site as catalytic or non-catalytic using the machine learning classifier MAHOMES II. HEAM more than quadruples the human site-level coverage of the largest prior metalloenzyme database. Using HEAM, we show that human metalloproteins are significantly enriched in KEGG disease pathways relative to the human proteome, and that metalloenzymes specifically are significantly enriched in ClinVar pathogenic variants — a distinction obscured in prior, catalytically unresolved metalloprotein datasets. These pathogenic variants are concentrated in metabolic disorders, indicating that metabolic dysfunction is a substantial contributor to metalloenzyme-linked disease. By pairing 3D structural annotation with catalytic classification, HEAM provides both a foundation for structure-guided drug design against metal-binding sites and a resource for determining how catalytic and non-catalytic metal function contribute to human disease.

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Biological foundation models encode rich information about protein structure, function, and cellular state in high-dimensional embeddings, but accessing specific biological properties typically relies on additional, task-specific prediction models. Here, we show that diverse biological properties can be mapped to interpretable, reusable directions in embedding space. In the Concept Activation Vector (CAV) approach, examples representing a concept are distinguished from a background set using a linear model, and the resulting weight vector defines the CAV for that concept. In protein embeddings, CAVs recover Gene Ontology and Enzyme Commission annotations, localize Pfam domains, reveal novel structural relationships, and capture DNA-binding and protein-interaction interface specificity. In single-cell embeddings, CAVs isolate cancer-associated expression transitions, and gene variation along these axes substantially agrees with conventional differential-expression analysis despite being a distinct computational approach. Together, these results establish concept directions as a common representation, enabling diverse biological features to be compared, localized, and manipulated.

We evaluate Geneformer, scBERT, scGPT, and scFoundation as frozen feature extractors for cell-type and perturbation-response prediction using layer-wise probes, leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) selection, readout controls, representation diagnostics, centered kernel alignment (CKA),…
items.abstract: Single-cell foundation models (scFMs) are commonly benchmarked using final-layer embeddings, although useful depth may depend on the task. We evaluate Geneformer, scBERT, scGPT, and scFoundation as frozen feature extractors for cell-type and perturbation-response prediction using layer-wise probes, leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) selection, readout controls, representation diagnostics, centered kernel alignment (CKA), and retrieval/collapse analyses. Intermediate layers significantly improve cell-type accuracy for scGPT and scBERT in several settings, while Geneformer and scFoundation generally show performance comparable to their final layers. For perturbation prediction, LODO identifies layer 1 as an earliest-on-par candidate across all four models, without establishing universal superiority. Paired scGPT CLS and mean-pooling analyses show that readout affects preferred depth. CKA and representation metrics reveal model- and task-dependent geometric changes, while retrieval and collapse checks support the robustness of perturbation findings. We recommend reporting extraction depth, readout, selection protocol, and task-specific diagnostics. A validated non-final layer may also reduce computation, although efficiency was not directly benchmarked.

items.abstract: Bloodstream infection (BSI) is a life-threatening condition where the risk of dying is affected by both patient- and pathogen-related factors. Certain microbial traits (e.g., virulence genes) are thought to affect survival rates from BSIs, but the magnitude of their impact on human mortality remains unclear. To address this, we analyzed the microbial genomes, quantitative proteomes, and electronic medical records (EMRs) from 35,746 BSIs from Calgary, Canada (2006-2022). We show that EMR-based machine learning models accurately predict 30-day mortality (AUC=0.83), but surprisingly, integrating >70,000 microbial genes/proteins does not improve this performance. We demonstrate that microbial factors co-segregate with specific patient cohorts and are therefore not independent predictors of risk. We conclude that microbial virulence factors have minimal impact on mortality rates from BSIs.

items.abstract: Background: Machine Learning (ML) has shown promise in histopathological diagnosis, but rare tumours, like duodenal epithelial neoplasms, are challenging because large, labelled datasets are difficult to assemble. We propose a data-efficient ML pipeline for detecting duodenal epithelial neoplasia in whole-slide images. Methods: We assembled a five-hospital dataset of haematoxylin and eosin-stained duodenal biopsy whole slide images (WSIs) at 10x magnification, comprising 8,027 normal and 401 neoplastic biopsies, including adenomas, carcinomas and neuroendocrine tumours. WSIs were divided into patches and encoded using the Hibou-B foundation model. We compared global standardisation with unsupervised site-specific standardisation of patch embeddings. Our pipeline combined principal component analysis, a Gaussian mixture model and a Random Forest classifier. We assessed generalisability using leave-one-hospital-out cross-validation across four hospitals and on an independent test set from a fifth hospital. Results: In leave-one-hospital-out cross-validation, the pipeline achieved a mean accuracy of 90%, sensitivity of 96%, specificity of 83% and an AUC of 0.96. On the external test hospital, it achieved 94% accuracy, 93% sensitivity, 95% specificity, and AUC of 0.97. Site-specific standardisation improved mean cross-validation accuracy by 20 percentage points compared with global standardisation, while the Gaussian mixture pipeline improved accuracy by 12 percentage points compared with mean pooling of patch embeddings. Conclusions: We present a data-efficient ML approach for detecting duodenal epithelial neoplasia from WSIs. Strong performance was maintained across hospitals and on an independent external test cohort despite the limited number of neoplastic training cases, supporting the feasibility of foundation-model-based approaches for rare histopathological diagnoses.

items.abstract: Background: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that significantly affect cognitive, academic, and social functioning. Although electroencephalography (EEG) has emerged as a promising non-invasive tool for identifying objective neurophysiological biomarkers of ADHD because of its high temporal resolution and cost-effectiveness, many existing machine learning studies rely on single-domain EEG features, which may not adequately capture the complex functional organization of the brain. Methods: This study proposes a subject-level EEG classification framework that integrates three complementary feature domains: spectral characteristics, weighted Phase Lag Index (wPLI)-based functional connectivity, and topological descriptors derived from persistent homology. EEG recordings from 121 subjects were preprocessed and segmented into overlapping windows for feature extraction. Window-level features were aggregated to generate subject-level representations. Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) was employed to select the 110 most informative features from an initial set of 1,043 descriptors. Five machine learning classifiers, including Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), were evaluated using stratified five-fold cross-validation. An ablation study was further conducted to assess the contribution of each feature domain. Model interpretability was investigated using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), two widely adopted Explainable Artificial Intelligence techniques for interpreting machine learning models. Results: Among the evaluated classifiers, the SVM achieved the highest classification performance, yielding an accuracy of 80.17%, an F1-score of 80.95%, a balanced accuracy of 80.14%, a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of 86.72%, and a precision recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) of 87.34%. The ablation study demonstrated that combining spectral, functional connectivity, and topological features consistently outperformed individual feature domains, highlighting the complementary nature of these representations. Explainable AI analyses further identified functional connectivity features as the primary contributors to classification performance while confirming the additional value of spectral and topological descriptors. Conclusions: The proposed framework demonstrates that integrating spectral analysis, functional connectivity, and topological data analysis provides an effective and interpretable approach for subject-level ADHD classification from EEG recordings. The combination of recursive feature selection, multi-domain feature fusion, ablation analysis, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence establishes a transparent and reproducible pipeline that may facilitate the development of reliable EEG-based clinical decision-support systems for ADHD.

items.abstract: Significance: There is potential for generative artificial intelligence (AI) to perform "full stack" academic publishing, including comprehensive manuscript fabrication, "peer"-review, and editorial decision making. This study evaluated the benefits and cautions in using AI for full stack academic publishing in clinical research about seizures. Methods: Three epileptologists each selected 1 published manuscript in Epilepsia and produced an AI-fabricated manuscript about seizures. AI tools were then used to perform "peer"-review and make editorial decisions with minimal human supervision. The rates of identifying AI-fabricated manuscripts and editorial decisions among the epileptologists was analyzed, and epileptologists' observations on how AI differed from typical human "peer"-review and editorial decisions was collected. Results: Four of 6 (67%) pairs of AI-fabricated and human-generated manuscripts were correctly identified. Only 1 AI-fabricated manuscript was editorially rejected, whereas another had a subtle indicator of fabrication. When compared to human content, AI generated content was comprehensive, detailed, and based on the highest standard of academic publication. However, generated content was more verbose, used more structured responses, and more critical feedback. Conclusions: These results demonstrate that the quality of AI-fabricated manuscripts about clinical research in seizures was sufficiently high that the current methods of peer and editorial review could not easily distinguish fabricated content compared to human-written content. Moreover, AI review and editorial decisions were high quality and appeared reasonable in many cases. AI tools have matured to the point that there should be thoughtful policies that permit AI assistance but prohibit insufficiently supervised autonomous scientific submissions, reviews, and editorial decisions.

items.abstract: Background: Relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) often progresses to secondary-progressive MS (SPMS), but diagnosis is typically retrospective, delaying potential interventions. Existing rule-based and machine learning approaches often lack prospective validation and provide no uncertainty estimates, limiting clinical adoption. Objective: To prospectively evaluate a conformal prediction (CP)-enabled random forest model for reproducing clinician-recorded disease course labels in the Swedish Multiple Sclerosis Registry (SMSReg) and compare its classifications with the Lorscheider criteria. Methods: The CP model was trained and calibrated on SMSReg-2022 (10,787 individuals, 85,461 hospital visits) and then validated on SMSReg-2025 (15,719 individuals, 45,077 hospital visits; not included in the SMSReg-2022 training/calibration/testing datasets). Performance was assessed at the hospital visit and individual levels and compared with the Lorscheider criteria. Results: The model maintained good calibration on the prospective dataset. At the per-hospital visit-level, the model accuracies were 92% (RRMS) and 95% (SPMS). At the individual level, sensitivity was 98%, specificity 89%, and F1-score 0.75. With clinician-recorded labels as reference, the model showed higher sensitivity than the Lorscheider criteria (98% vs. 71%), more transition assignments (90% vs. 57%), and higher F1-score (0.76 vs. 0.69). Conclusion: The CP-enabled model prospectively reproduced clinician-recorded disease course labels with calibrated uncertainty, supporting harmonization and decision support.

items.abstract: Introduction: Early Alzheimer's disease (AD) staging remains challenging because clinical categories and global amyloid PET measures provide only coarse characterization of disease progression. We developed a continuous amyloid staging score from regional amyloid PET to complement global amyloid burden. Methods: : Using longitudinal florbetapir PET from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), we trained an end-to-end deep learning model to directly estimate a continuous amyloid staging score. We evaluated longitudinal consistency, its relationship with global amyloid burden, regional contributors to early-stage variation, and whether the staging score stratified subsequent memory decline among participants matched for baseline global amyloid burden. Cognitive analyses were replicated in A4+LEARN. Results: : The staging score better preserved longitudinal visit order than existing amyloid staging approaches. During early disease stages, it captured regional amyloid variation despite relatively stable global amyloid burden. Among participants with similar baseline global amyloid burden, higher staging scores were associated with faster subsequent memory decline in both ADNI and A4+LEARN. Discussion: A continuous amyloid staging score complements global amyloid burden for early AD staging and cognitive risk stratification. Keywords: Alzheimer's disease; amyloid PET; disease staging; cognitive decline

items.abstract: Abstract Background Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is managed primarily with respiratory-based algorithms, even though cardiovascular comorbidity is a major determinant of adverse outcomes. We aimed to identify and characterise cardiopulmonary phenotypes defined by exacerbator profile and cardiovascular risk (CVR) in patients with COPD managed in primary care. Methods Cross-sectional, multicentre, retrospective study of 1,307 patients with COPD across 52 primary care centres in six Spanish regions. Phenotypes cross-classified the exacerbator profile (GOLD) with cardiovascular burden (established cardiovascular disease [CVD] / high risk / low-to-moderate risk). We used mixed-effects logistic regression, intraclass correlation, ROC curves, collinearity analysis and a preliminary unsupervised clustering analysis (machine learning). Results Median age was 72.6 years; 65.7% were men, 58.8% had moderate airflow obstruction, 31.2% were exacerbators and 36.8% had established CVD. The most frequent phenotype was the non-exacerbator with high CVR (40.6%), whereas the exacerbator phenotype with established CVD carried the greatest burden of hospitalisations and disease severity. We identified a hidden-risk phenotype—non-exacerbators with CVD—with a higher risk of hospitalisation and poorer clinical control (adjusted OR 1.99; 95% CI 1.21–3.25; p = 0.006 vs non-exacerbator phenotypes; sensitivity analysis). Clustering confirmed the clinical findings. Conclusions In COPD, jointly considering exacerbations and cardiovascular burden defines clinically relevant phenotypes, including a hidden-risk group of non-exacerbators with CVD. These practical, readily available axes complement the eosinophil count and support an integrated cardiopulmonary assessment.

items.abstract: Abstract This study proposes an automated method for detecting tooth positions and predicting full-mouth series (FMS) radiograph placement using oriented object detection and Siamese neural networks. A total of 5,431 radiographs from 354 patients were annotated and used to train deep learning models. Oriented bounding boxes were generated using a YOLOv5 detector, followed by tooth numbering, feature extraction, and image classification via a multitask ResNet50 model. FMS placement was predicted using a Siamese neural network inspired by jigsaw-puzzle tasks, with permutation-based training and patient-level five-fold cross-validation. Mean tooth-numbering accuracy was 0.99 ± 0.00. Mean FMS-placement accuracy was 0.97 ± 0.01 for upper left and right periapical radiographs, 0.98 ± 0.02 for upper anterior periapical radiographs, 0.98 ± 0.01 for lower left and right periapical radiographs, 0.99 ± 0.01 for lower anterior periapical radiographs, and 0.96 ± 0.02 for bitewing radiographs; overall mean accuracy was 0.98 ± 0.01. This internally tested AI pipeline demonstrated high accuracy for tooth numbering and automated FMS arrangement and may help streamline dental radiographic workflows, subject to external and clinical validation.

items.abstract: Abstract Patients considering robot-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP) require information that spans diagnosis, treatment selection, functional recovery, and recurrence surveillance. We compared the quality of English-language RARP patient education generated by ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Doubao. Twenty-five questions covering screening, diagnosis, treatment decision-making, perioperative care, rehabilitation, and follow-up were submitted individually to each model, yielding 75 responses. Three blinded clinicians evaluated the responses using the Global Quality Score, modified DISCERN, Quality Analysis of Medical Artificial Intelligence, Ensuring Quality Information for Patients, and the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool; six readability indices were also calculated. Overall Global Quality Scores did not differ significantly across models. ChatGPT achieved a higher EQIP score (median, 75.00%) than DeepSeek and Doubao (65.83% each) and greater PEMAT actionability (59.00% vs. 54.33% and 47.67%, respectively). DeepSeek generated comparatively easier-to-read text, although all three models exceeded commonly recommended sixth- to eighth-grade reading levels for public-facing health materials. Under the majority-rater criterion, no factual errors or outdated recommendations were identified, whereas key omissions occurred mainly in DeepSeek and Doubao responses. Inter-rater agreement was low, indicating substantial uncertainty in multidimensional human assessment. LLMs may support the preparation of clinician-reviewed RARP educational materials but should not replace individualized counseling by urologists.

items.abstract: Abstract Hip fractures cause substantial morbidity and mortality in older adults. Sarcopenia is a key modifiable risk factor, yet few models integrate CT-derived muscle-fat metrics with clinical data. This study aimed to develop a risk prediction model for elderly hip fractures, compare multiple machine learning algorithms, and convert the optimal model into an interpretable nomogram. This prospective cohort enrolled patients aged ≥ 60 years undergoing hip CT, including fracture cases and controls. Muscle/fat area, mean attenuation, and skeletal muscle index were measured at femoral head, lesser trochanter, and L3. The cohort was split 7:3 into training and validation sets. Eight classifiers were built using Boruta-selected features, with performance assessed by AUC, calibration, and decision curve analysis (DCA). The logistic regression (LR) achieved the highest AUC (0.779). Multivariable regression retained eight independent predictors: age, elevated glucose, osteoporosis, fat area1/2, muscle mean2, SMI1, and SMI3. The nomogram incorporating these variables showed good discrimination (training AUC = 0.826; validation AUC = 0.817), favorable calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow P = 0.647 and 0.412, respectively), and clinical net benefit on DCA. LR performed comparably or better than other ML algorithms. The nomogram offers a simple, interpretable tool for individualized hip fracture risk stratification using eight routinely available parameters.

items.abstract: Abstract Objective To develop an artificial intelligence (AI) model based on ResNet and Hill classification of gastroesophageal flap valve (GEFV) for endoscopic diagnosis of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and reduce the subjectivity of manual grading, and provide decision support for clinical GERD risk stratification and anti-reflux therapy selection. Methods In this single-center retrospective diagnostic accuracy study, 7,652 endoscopic images from patients with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) were split into training, validation, and test sets at a patient-level 7:2:1 ratio. A ResNet-152 model was trained with class-weighted cross-entropy loss. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, and F1-score. Correlation with mean lower esophageal sphincter (LES) pressure from high-resolution manometry (HRM) was assessed in an independent cohort of 92 patients. Results Inter-observer agreement among expert endoscopists yielded a weighted Kappa of 0.73. The final model achieved an overall test-set accuracy of 85.02%, with per-grade accuracies of 84.76%, 80.95%, 76.19%, and 72.38% for Hill grades I–IV, respectively. All global performance metrics exceeded 0.8. And the model significantly outperformed junior endoscopists on a random test subset ( P < 0.01). AI-predicted Hill grades showed a significant negative correlation with mean resting LES pressure (Spearman's ρ=−0.501, P < 0.001). Conclusions The ResNet-152 model demonstrated reliable performance for automated GEFV Hill classification and correlates significantly with objective manometric parameters. This AI tool has potential as a clinical decision-support system to standardize esophagogastric junction morphological assessment in GERD.

items.abstract: Abstract Background Pre-existing antibodies to Plasmodium vivax may cross-react with P. knowlesi and influence infection outcomes. We investigated whether baseline P. vivax antibody levels affect parasitaemia and clearance in knowlesi malaria. Methods Total IgG to 21 P. vivax antigens was quantified in pre-treatment plasma from patients in three Malaysian clinical trials. Parasitaemia was assessed 6-hourly by microscopy and clearance half-life estimated. Antibody associations with P. knowlesi baseline parasitaemia and clearance were identified using regression and machine learning approaches (elastic net regression and random forests). Results Data were available for 134 patients (median age 37 years, 37% with prior malaria). Five antibodies were associated with reduced baseline P. knowlesi parasitaemia (0.75–0.90-fold lower per two-fold increase, 95% CIs ranging from 0.65–1.00). Median P. knowlesi parasite clearance half-life was 2.6 hours (IQR 2.1–3.2). Two antibodies were associated with slightly slower parasite clearance (1.04-fold increases in mean clearance half-life per two-fold antibody level). Within-group correlation analyses revealed widespread, positive antibody associations in P. knowlesi infections, with weaker but coordinated (RBP and DBP family) responses in malaria-negative endemic controls. Conclusions Cross-reactive P. vivax antibodies may partially constrain P. knowlesi parasitaemia, but functional studies are needed to clarify their role in immunity and zoonotic transmission.

items.abstract: Abstract Patients with peripheral artery disease (PAD), chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI), and/or diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) are at increased risk for limb loss and death. Existing risk calculators lack consistent clinical adoption; therefore, we aimed to identify vascular and non-vascular predictors of revascularization, amputation, and cardiovascular death using data from the OMOP CDM plus vascular extension. We assembled a cohort of adults with PAD, CLTI, or DFU receiving care within the UNC Health System from 2014–2024 (n = 178,995). Using 127 vascular-specific and thousands of non-vascular HER variables, we used logistic regression with inverse probability weighting and MCMC-based dimensionality reduction to predict revascularization, amputation, and cardiovascular death. The mean age was 72.5 ± 13.9 years; 50.9% were female and 23.5% Black. The revascularization and amputation models performed well (AUC = 0.984 and 0.926, respectively), while cardiovascular mortality prediction was modest (AUC = 0.772). Revascularization predictors were dominated by arterial disease, amputation prediction was driven by treatment interactions with dementia and frailty, and cardiovascular events and risk factors were the strongest predictors of cardiovascular mortality. Prediction models derived from harmonized EHR data demonstrated strong performance for revascularization and amputation. These findings support harmonized EHR-based vascular prediction modeling and warrant multi-institutional validation.
